entries.t: Status hidden in a pile of flags
entries.p: Find implicit state machines where a feature's lifecycle is scattered across separate boolean flags, conditionals, and UI checks instead of one explicit status. Identify reachable invalid combinations and unclear transitions.
entries.why: Finds features whose real status is spread across a pile of yes/no flags, so combinations that should be impossible can happen.
entries.ev: For each affected feature, its flags and transitions (file:line), plus at least one concrete reachable invalid combination showing how a user or system event produces it.
entries.skip: Features already use a single explicit status enum checked in one place.
entries.tools: Repository access only.
entries.blind: Do not flag every boolean field as a state machine. Report only flag combinations that are actually reachable and cause bugs.
entries.line: Finds features tracking status through scattered yes/no flags (`isPaid`, `isCancelled`, `isPending`) that allow impossible combinations to happen.

entries.p: Trace one core business concept end to end across the UI, API, database schema, and background jobs. If I did not name a specific concept, pick the single most central entity in this product and state which one you chose. Find every place its meaning, fields, nullability, or validation rules shift between layers.
entries.why: Shows where one word (a task, a fund, a run) means slightly different things in different parts of the app.
entries.ev: One table for that concept listing each layer, its name/type/column, its validation rules, and file:line, with every mismatch clearly flagged.
entries.skip: A simple concept that exists in only one layer of the app.
entries.tools: Repository access and read-only access to the database layout.
entries.blind: Tracing five concepts at once produces a vague essay. Keep the trace tightly focused on one concept.
entries.line: Checks whether one core business word (like "order", "project", or "member") means slightly different things in the UI, API, database, and background jobs.

entries.t: Layers that don't earn their keep
entries.p: Find code abstractions that add indirection without real benefit: single-use wrappers, generic factories, deep inheritance, and pass-through utilities that make changes harder to follow than plain direct code. Separate dead weight from thin adapters that legitimately isolate an unstable third-party SDK or create a test boundary.
entries.why: Finds extra layers of code you could delete so the code, and the agents reading it, get simpler.
entries.ev: Each removal candidate (file:line), how many callers it has, what deleting it would inline or simplify, and which tests would update.
entries.skip: A small, direct codebase or one that just went through a cleanup pass.
entries.tools: Repository access only.
entries.blind: Do not flag thin boundary wrappers around external payment, email, or AI SDKs as useless — those protect against vendor changes.
entries.line: Identifies unnecessary wrappers, factories, and pass-through helpers you can delete so the codebase is smaller and easier for agents to edit safely.

entries.p: Find places where the same fact is stored in more than one place — across database tables, derived columns, caches, browser storage, or external services like billing or search. For each pair, trace which copy is authoritative, how they stay in sync, what sequence of failures makes them diverge, and which copies actually earn their keep for speed or history.
entries.why: Finds data kept in two places (a saved copy and a table, the browser and the server) that can quietly disagree.
entries.ev: Each duplicated fact with its authoritative source and copies (file:line), how updates propagate, a concrete failure sequence that causes drift, and whether the extra copy should stay or be removed.
entries.skip: Every fact lives in one place, or caches are rebuilt cleanly on every read.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only database access.
entries.line: Finds facts stored in two places (database vs. Stripe, table vs. cache, client state vs. server) that can quietly drift out of sync.

entries.t: Old design choices that now cost you
entries.p: Examine the codebase and git history for early architectural choices that were reasonable when the project started and now create measurable friction: recurring bugs, repeated workarounds, or slow feature work. Separate real operational liabilities from out-of-fashion tech preferences.
entries.why: Separates old design choices that now cost real time or bugs from ones that are only out of fashion.
entries.ev: Each architectural liability with its original rationale, concrete evidence of today's cost (repeated bug fixes, workarounds, slow paths, or commits), and the smallest practical path forward.
entries.skip: A brand-new codebase under a couple of months old with little change history.
entries.tools: Repository and its git history.
entries.line: Pinpoints early technical shortcuts that made sense on day one and now cause recurring bugs, workarounds, or slow delivery.

entries.t: Code that relies on lucky timing
entries.p: Find asynchronous operations whose correctness relies on events arriving in a lucky order without an explicit lock, sequence check, or state guard. Trace scheduling, retries, cancellation, and concurrent writes; reproduce the highest-risk case and propose the smallest enforceable contract.
entries.why: Finds code that only works because things usually happen in the right order.
entries.ev: Each assumed ordering, what real-world event can break it (retry, slow network, double click, webhook burst), and a reproducible case for the highest-risk bug.
entries.skip: Strictly sequential scripts with no concurrent requests, timers, webhooks, or background tasks.
entries.tools: Repository; a way to run the code locally to reproduce the problem.
entries.line: Finds background steps, requests, or UI events that silently assume one thing finishes before another without enforcing it.

entries.p: Map external side effects and resource lifecycles across this application: connections, subscriptions, listeners, timers, streams, cache entries and background workers. Find unclear ownership, incomplete cleanup and operations that outlive their intended scope. Prioritize evidenced leaks or correctness risks over stylistic patterns.
entries.why: Finds timers, listeners and connections that nobody clearly owns or shuts off.
entries.ev: Each resource with where it is created, who should release it, and the path where it is not released.
entries.skip: Short-lived scripts and one-off server functions that keep nothing running between calls.
entries.tools: Repository access; memory snapshots help confirm.

entries.line: Traces every way someone creates an account, signs in, resets a password, switches devices, or deletes an account, and finds where people can get locked out or keep access they shouldn't have.
entries.p: Trace the full account lifecycle in this application: sign-up, email verification, password sign-in, magic links, OAuth/social login, password reset, email change, session refresh and expiry, sign-out, role or team revocation, and account deletion. Look for ways a real person gets stuck or locked out (expired links with no resend button, case-sensitive email mismatches, OAuth colliding with an existing password account, redirect loops after sign-in, sessions dropping on refresh) and ways revoked users keep access (cached tokens, active sessions that survive password change or removal). Check both code and auth provider configuration where visible in the repo.
entries.ev: A walkthrough of each account flow with file:line, every lockout or leftover-access failure found, and any auth provider settings that live outside the repo and need my check in a named dashboard.
entries.skip: A public tool or static site with no accounts or sign-in.
entries.blind: Agents test only the happy sign-in path. Trace duplicate emails across sign-in methods, expired tokens, and what happens to open browser tabs after a user is removed or changes their password.
entries.why: Traces every way someone creates an account, signs in, resets a password, switches devices, or deletes an account, and finds where people can get locked out or keep access they shouldn't have.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.t: Screens that fight how people work
entries.p: Map this product's pages, routes, and navigation against the real jobs users come to do. Look for pages that should merge, shrink into a tab or panel, or go away; competing menus pointing to the same destinations; and workflows users must piece together across multiple screens. State clearly whether the underlying page structure causes two or more of these issues; if not, keep the structure and recommend local fixes.
entries.why: Finds when confusing screens are a symptom of how the product is organised rather than a list of separate bugs.
entries.ev: A verdict per page (keep, merge, demote, or retire) with evidence, the two to five root causes behind user confusion, and today's site map beside the proposed one.
entries.skip: A tiny app with fewer than five screens, or a navigation redesign that just shipped with no user feedback yet.
entries.tools: Repository; the app running locally with test accounts for the browser checks.
entries.blind: Do not propose a full redesign for isolated screen bugs. Recommend structural changes only when one cause explains multiple problems.
entries.aka: Structure that fights the users' work
entries.line: Checks whether confusing screens are caused by how pages and menus are organized overall, then proposes a cleaner site map if the structure itself is the problem.

entries.p: Trace and measure the five slowest or heaviest user journeys from browser interaction to database response. Look for unnecessary network round trips, sequential waterfalls, slow queries, repeated work, heavy synchronous handlers blocking other requests, and quadratic loops over growing collections. Measure each step's share of total latency before ranking fixes.
entries.why: Shows where the seconds go on the paths people actually use.
entries.ev: A measured timing breakdown per journey (browser network timing, server timing, query plan, or event-loop delay) showing each step's share of total time, ranked by impact.
entries.skip: Every main flow already feels fast and server/database bills are flat.
entries.tools: Browser developer tools or Playwright recordings, server logs or timing data, and the database's query plan (EXPLAIN).
entries.blind: Reading code statically guesses at latency and flags tiny loops that never matter. Require actual measurements at realistic data sizes before ranking anything.
entries.line: Measures your five slowest user flows from button click to database reply and pinpoints which steps burn the most time.

entries.t: Steps that wait for no reason
entries.p: Audit asynchronous hot paths for two opposite problems: (1) independent operations waiting sequentially when they could safely run in parallel without breaking ordering, rate limits, or database transaction boundaries, and (2) parallel fan-outs or queues running with no concurrency cap that could exhaust connection pools, memory, or external API limits at realistic scale.
entries.why: Finds steps that wait for each other to finish when they could run at the same time.
entries.ev: For each sequential chain, the current measured duration, why the steps are independent, and any shared transaction or rate limit to respect; for each unbounded fan-out, its maximum width on realistic data next to the downstream limit and a recommended cap.
entries.skip: Fast paths finishing in a few milliseconds, or fixed tiny lists with no external or database pressure.
entries.tools: Repository; a timing script to measure the result afterward.
entries.blind: Wrapping awaits in Promise.all breaks when calls share a single database transaction or hit a rate-limited API. Check transaction scopes, pool sizes, and vendor rate limits before recommending parallelism.
entries.line: Finds slow chains of steps running one after another that could safely run together, as well as parallel batches with no cap that could overload your database or APIs.

entries.p: Find database queries whose execution cost grows disproportionately as rows, users, tenants, or relationships increase. Inspect query plans, missing or unused indexes, N+1 joins, unbounded pagination, and filtering done in application memory instead of the database.
entries.why: Finds the database queries that will be the first to slow down as tables grow.
entries.ev: Each suspect query (file:line), its EXPLAIN ANALYZE output (or query plan) at realistic row counts, the exact scaling bottleneck, and the proposed index or query rewrite. If a safe non-production copy exists, note whether the rewrite can be benchmarked there in a follow-up step.
entries.skip: Projects with only tiny, fixed-size tables (such as settings or short lookup lists).
entries.tools: Read-only database access with EXPLAIN (the database's query plan). A Neon or Supabase branch copy for anything heavier.
entries.line: Identifies database queries that are fine with sample data and will bog down as rows, users, or accounts pile up.

entries.p: Find expensive computations, queries, API calls, or UI renders that run repeatedly even though their inputs have not changed. Measure how often each runs and what it costs before considering caching, memoization, batching, or incremental updates.
entries.why: Finds work redone on every request or screen redraw when nothing it depends on changed.
entries.ev: Each repeated operation (file:line), how often it runs, how often its inputs actually change, its measured cost, and — if you recommend caching — exactly how and when that cache gets invalidated.
entries.skip: Operations that are already cheap, where caching would add stale-data bugs for negligible gain.
entries.tools: A profiler or request logs to count repeats.
entries.blind: Every cache creates a second source of truth. Reject any caching proposal that cannot explain invalidation cleanly.
entries.line: Spots expensive calculations, fetches, or renders that rerun on every click or request even when their inputs never changed.

entries.t: What breaks at ten times the size
entries.p: Model what happens when this product's stored data and concurrent active users grow tenfold. Use real table counts, request rates, query plans, and hosting/database plan limits to identify the first bottlenecks that break or spike cost.
entries.why: Names the first thing to break if the project takes off, before it does.
entries.ev: Current baseline sizes and rates (marking anything estimated), projected 10x numbers, the exact ceiling each bottleneck hits (connection pool, query time, storage quota, rate limit, or plan tier), and the threshold at which you should actually fix it.
entries.skip: A personal tool or fixed-audience app with flat usage and no growth expected.
entries.tools: Database stats, hosting plan limits, current traffic numbers.
entries.line: Projects your current numbers tenfold to show which database limit, hosting cap, or code bottleneck fails first if growth takes off.

entries.t: Loops that blow up with big data
entries.p: Identify potentially quadratic or worse operations in frequently used code paths, including nested joins in application memory, copy-on-every-iteration patterns and repeated scans. Determine realistic input sizes and benchmark the highest-impact candidates before changing their algorithms.
entries.why: Finds loops inside loops that are fine at 50 rows and painful at 50,000.
entries.ev: Each candidate with realistic input size and a benchmark at that size; ignore candidates whose real inputs stay small.
entries.skip: Code whose inputs are small and capped by design.
entries.tools: A speed-test setup. The experimental agent-complexity-optimizer scanner can suggest places to look.
entries.blind: Static scanners flag nested loops over tiny arrays. Without real sizes the list is mostly noise.

entries.p: Investigate sustained memory growth and leaked resources across the browser and server: unbounded caches, unremoved event listeners, timers and intervals never cleared, unclosed database or network connections, leaked streams or subscriptions, detached DOM nodes, and retained closures or request payloads. Validate top suspects with repeatable growth checks or heap snapshots where available.
entries.why: Finds why a page or process gets slower or crashes the longer it runs.
entries.ev: Each leak or unclosed resource with where it is created (file:line), who should clean it up, the path where cleanup is skipped, and heap-snapshot or growth evidence for the top suspects.
entries.skip: Short-lived scripts or stateless functions with flat memory usage over time.
entries.tools: Chrome DevTools memory snapshots or Node --inspect.
entries.line: Finds unclosed timers, listeners, connections, and growing caches that make a tab or server sluggish or crash the longer it stays running.

entries.t: One slow step that blocks the rest
entries.p: Find synchronous work performed in latency-sensitive asynchronous handlers, including filesystem operations, parsing, compression, large serialization and CPU-heavy transforms. Measure event-loop impact and identify safe offloading, batching or scheduling fixes.
entries.why: Finds one slow step that makes every other request wait in line behind it.
entries.ev: Event-loop delay or long-task measurements tied to the specific handler.
entries.skip: Background scripts where nothing else shares the process.
entries.tools: Node profiler or the browser's Performance panel.

entries.p: Examine places where work is parallelized or queued without explicit limits. Find cases where a speed optimization could overwhelm rate limits, memory, connection pools or a downstream service; propose and test concurrency bounds with realistic load.
entries.why: Finds work run in parallel with no limit, which can swamp the database connections or an outside service.
entries.ev: Each fan-out with its maximum width at realistic input, the downstream limit, and a load test with a bound.
entries.skip: Parallel work over a fixed, small list.
entries.tools: Repository; a load-testing script pointed at a non-production copy.

entries.p: Find write operations, webhooks, imports, and user actions that cannot safely run twice or resume after an interruption. Examine duplicate requests, webhook retries, out-of-order arrivals, idempotency keys, unique constraints, and transaction boundaries. Do not assume an ON CONFLICT clause alone guarantees safe reruns; check side effects like emails, charges, and counters too.
entries.why: Finds actions that do damage when they run twice: double sends, double charges, duplicate rows.
entries.ev: Each unsafe operation (file:line), what triggers a retry or duplicate, what happens on a second run, and whether a key, constraint, or lock currently prevents damage.
entries.skip: Read-only apps that never write records, send messages, or charge cards.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only access to the database layout.
entries.line: Finds actions — charges, emails, webhooks, imports, and form submits — that cause double-billing, duplicate sends, or corrupted rows if retried.

entries.t: Fallbacks that look like real data
entries.p: Trace every place the application quietly substitutes a default, zero, null, stale value, or empty list when a request, query, or calculation fails. Determine whether a user could mistake that fallback for valid, up-to-date information.
entries.why: Finds screens that show a confident zero or an empty list when the real answer is 'we could not load this'.
entries.ev: Each silent fallback with its trigger, what appears on screen, and whether anything alerts the user that loading failed.
entries.skip: Every error path already displays a clear error or unavailable state on screen.
entries.tools: Repository; the app running to see what users see.
entries.line: Finds places where an error quietly turns into a normal-looking zero, empty list, or stale value so users never know loading failed.

entries.p: Identify critical business invariants this product assumes (such as non-negative balances, unique ownership, valid status combinations, or plan limits) that are enforced only in UI code or never enforced at all. Recommend the right enforcement layer (database constraint, schema validation, or server check) and write a test demonstrating how the top rule can be broken today.
entries.why: Finds the rules everyone assumes (one owner per task, no negative balance) that nothing actually checks.
entries.ev: Each unenforced rule, where the app assumes it (file:line), where it should be enforced, and a failing test proving it can be violated today.
entries.skip: Core rules are already enforced by database constraints and server-side checks.
entries.tools: Repository; a test database or branch copy.
entries.line: Uncovers core business rules everyone assumes are true (such as "no negative balance" or "one owner per account") that neither the server nor database actually blocks.

entries.p: Audit how this application handles dates and time: time zones, daylight saving transitions, day boundaries, expirations, scheduled jobs, client-versus-server clock skew, and historical date queries.
entries.why: Finds the date bugs that show up twice a year, at midnight, or in another time zone.
entries.ev: Each time-sensitive path with the time zone it assumes, plus a failing test at a daylight saving change and around midnight in both UTC and your users' primary time zone.
entries.skip: Features that never store, compare, schedule, or display dates or times.
entries.tools: Repository; tests with the clock fixed to a set time.
entries.line: Hunts down date and clock bugs around midnight, daylight saving shifts, expirations, and users in other time zones.

entries.p: Find race conditions and lost-update paths across concurrent UI edits, API calls, caches, webhooks, and background jobs. Prove real risks with a concrete reproduction instead of listing theoretical possibilities.
entries.why: Finds updates that overwrite newer data because two things wrote at once.
entries.ev: Each confirmed race (file:line) with a runnable test or script that reproduces the lost update.
entries.skip: Single-user records written by only one synchronous code path.
entries.tools: Repository; a local or branch-copy database to reproduce the problem.
entries.blind: Agents list theoretical race conditions freely. Count only races backed by a concrete reproduction or an exact reachable sequence.
entries.line: Finds places where two tabs, users, webhooks, or jobs edit the same record at once and the slower one silently wipes out the newer change.

entries.p: Trace error, timeout, and cancellation paths for database transactions, locks, file handles, temporary files, background jobs, and external network calls. Find paths that leave resources held open or data half-committed when something fails midway, and demonstrate the highest-risk case with controlled failure injection where practical.
entries.why: Finds what is left behind when something fails halfway.
entries.ev: Each failure path, what gets left half-committed or held open, and a reproduction for the highest-risk case.
entries.skip: Simple stateless endpoints or scripts that perform a single atomic read or write with no multi-step state.
entries.tools: Repository; a way to force errors in tests.
entries.line: Traces what gets left stuck or half-saved when an action crashes, times out, or gets cancelled midway.

entries.t: Lost place: Back, refresh and shared links
entries.p: Check whether this application preserves the user's place. In a local or staging browser (never production with real accounts), open lists, filters, tabs, modals, and detail records, then test Back, Forward, page refresh, opening links in a new tab, and opening copied URLs in a fresh session both signed out and as another user. Trace every lost filter, scroll jump, wiped draft, broken Back action, or wrong landing screen to the code that owns that state.
entries.why: Finds the everyday friction where Back closes the wrong thing, a filter resets, or a pasted link opens the wrong view.
entries.ev: Each tested journey (start, action, expected result, observed result) with the file:line owning the state and a clear PASS or FAIL verdict.
entries.skip: A simple static site with no filters, panels, drafts, or signed-in views.
entries.tools: The app running locally or on staging with test accounts; Playwright, which the plugin looks for and asks before installing.
entries.blind: Even ordinary page loads can trigger background writes in some apps. Run browser checks only against local development or safe staging test accounts.
entries.line: Tests Back, Forward, page refresh, new tabs, and shared URLs to find where filters reset, drafts disappear, or pasted links land on the wrong screen.

entries.t: Unit tests that give false comfort
entries.p: Find critical user journeys that have extensive unit-test coverage but insufficient evidence that they work end to end. Strengthen the smallest set of tests that closes the real gaps.
entries.why: Finds features whose automated checks all pass and that still break for real people.
entries.ev: Each journey with what the tests cover, what they skip (real auth, real DB, real browser), and the one added check.
entries.skip: User paths already covered by a browser test.
entries.tools: Playwright or the in-app browser for the full start-to-finish check.

entries.p: Find tests that would continue passing if the underlying feature stopped working. Examine mocks, fixtures, assertions, and tests that merely reproduce implementation details.
entries.why: Finds tests that pass no matter what.
entries.ev: For each suspect test, break the feature on purpose and show the test still passes.
entries.skip: Brand-new test suites written before the code.
entries.tools: Repository and the test runner.

entries.p: Trace every untrusted external input — forms, URL parameters, file uploads, headers, webhooks, and AI model outputs — from entry point to sensitive operations (database writes, auth changes, billing, file access, admin actions, outbound requests). Check for missing authorization or ownership checks, tenant isolation gaps, injection vectors, and unsafe parsing.
entries.why: Follows input from outsiders to the places it can do harm.
entries.ev: Each risky path listing its entry point, checks along the way, the sensitive operation reached, and the exact missing safeguard (file:line).
entries.skip: A completely static site with zero backend endpoints, forms, uploads, webhooks, or stored user data.
entries.tools: Repository access.
entries.line: Traces every form field, upload, URL parameter, webhook, and AI output from entry to sensitive actions to find missing permission or safety checks.

entries.p: Audit dependency and CI supply-chain exposure: known security advisories matching installed versions, package install scripts, GitHub Actions or CI workflows triggered by untrusted pull requests, overly broad workflow permissions, and which jobs can read deployment secrets.
entries.why: Checks what a harmful outside package or pull request could reach.
entries.ev: Active advisories matched to installed versions, packages with lifecycle install scripts, workflow permission gaps (file:line), and a map of which CI jobs can access which secrets.
entries.skip: A zero-dependency repository with no automated CI or deployment workflows.
entries.tools: The lockfile (exact package list), automated build workflow files, npm audit or the auditor skill.
entries.line: Audits installed third-party packages and automated GitHub/CI workflows for known vulnerabilities, risky install scripts, and overly broad secret permissions.

entries.p: Audit every authentication, authorization, rate-limit, and webhook-signature check for fail-open behavior: cases where a missing environment variable, null user object, thrown exception, network timeout, or malformed request results in access being granted instead of denied.
entries.why: Finds security checks that let people in when something goes wrong.
entries.ev: Each security gate (file:line) and what happens on missing config, thrown error, and malformed input, backed by a code trace or safe test request.
entries.skip: A public static app with no authentication, permissions, private endpoints, or webhooks.
entries.tools: Repository; the app running locally in demo mode.
entries.line: Finds sign-in, permission, or webhook checks that accidentally let people through when a setting is missing, a service errors out, or a request is malformed.

entries.p: Audit the test suite covering this product's critical user journeys. Look for three failure modes: (1) heavy unit-test coverage that mocks away real auth, database, or browser behavior so broken integrations still pass, (2) assertions that test implementation details or cannot fail meaningfully when user behavior breaks, and (3) critical flows with no end-to-end check at all. For the single highest-risk gap, write one independent test that would catch a real user-facing regression.
entries.why: Asks what each test really proves, then adds one check that would catch a real break.
entries.ev: For each critical journey, what existing tests actually exercise versus what they mock or skip (file:line), any toothless tests found and why they pass on broken code, and the one added check for the top gap.
entries.skip: Every critical user flow is already covered by end-to-end checks that run against real storage and have caught real regressions.
entries.tools: Repository and test runner.
entries.line: Checks what your tests actually prove about key user flows, exposes mocked-out or toothless tests that still pass when features break, and adds one real check for the biggest gap.
entries.blind: Do not modify application code to "test the tests." Prove toothless assertions by tracing the mocked boundary or writing an independent test against the real requirement.

entries.p: Audit configuration and environment variables across local development, CI, preview, and production. Find ambiguous fallbacks, test-mode switches that could stay on, fail-open permissions, and behavior that silently changes when a variable is unset. Check actual code and deployment config files instead of trusting README examples. Never print or expose secret values.
entries.why: Finds settings that behave differently in production than anyone expects.
entries.ev: A table of environment-sensitive settings (variable names only, never values), where each is read (file:line), its fallback when missing, and what breaks or shifts across environments.
entries.skip: A local-only tool with a single environment and no deployment settings.
entries.tools: Vercel settings list (names only, never values), automated build config, the code that reads each setting.
entries.blind: Never print secret values in output or logs. Report only variable names, code paths, and whether a setting exists.
entries.line: Compares local, preview, and production configuration to catch missing environment variables and defaults that behave differently once live.

entries.p: Inventory the development environment's browser runtimes, caches, SDKs, package managers, and duplicate installations. Identify obsolete or wasteful components, assess dependencies, and propose a safe cleanup.
entries.why: Finds disk space and confusion spent on duplicate developer tools and stale saved files on your computer.
entries.ev: Each component with size, version, what depends on it, and whether deleting it is safe and reversible.
entries.skip: When disk space is fine and builds are stable.
entries.tools: A terminal on your computer.
entries.blind: Treat every deletion as a proposal. Shared runtimes break other apps silently.

entries.t: Why production might not match main
entries.p: Trace a code change from merge to live users: build steps, database migrations, deployment triggers, CDN or app caches, background workers, and mobile/client updates. Identify every point where a deploy step can silently skip, fail, or serve stale code without alerting anyone.
entries.why: Lists every way 'merged' can fail to mean 'live'.
entries.ev: The actual release pipeline step by step with its config files (file:line), and for each step how it can fail or stay stale silently.
entries.skip: You already mapped this pipeline recently and nothing in hosting, builds, or migrations changed since.
entries.tools: Automated build and Vercel config, deployment history (read-only).
entries.line: Traces every step from merging code to users seeing it live, exposing caches, manual deploys, or skipped migrations that leave production stale.

entries.p: Analyze CI and deployment workflows against the real failures they catch. Look for duplicated build/install steps, missing caches, redundant checks, and expensive jobs that add little confidence over faster checks.
entries.why: Finds paid automated-check minutes spent on checks that never catch anything.
entries.ev: Each CI job (file:line) with its typical duration, run frequency, whether recent runs caught real bugs (where run history is accessible), and the highest-impact speedup or cut.
entries.skip: CI runs finish in a minute or two and cost nothing.
entries.tools: GitHub Actions run history via gh.
entries.line: Reviews your automated CI checks to spot slow, expensive, or duplicated jobs that burn minutes without catching real bugs.

entries.t: Background jobs that hang or stop halfway
entries.p: Audit every scheduled job, cron task, and background worker for hangs, overlapping runs, partial updates, missing timeouts, unsafe retries, and deploy interruptions.
entries.why: Finds scheduled jobs and background workers that can hang, overlap or stop halfway.
entries.ev: Each job (file:line) with its schedule or trigger, timeout, lock/overlap protection, what happens if it crashes midway, and how a failure is reported.
entries.skip: Projects with no scheduled tasks, queues, or background workers.
entries.tools: Repository, the scheduled jobs in vercel.json, logs.
entries.line: Audits scheduled tasks and background queues to see what happens when a job hangs, overlaps with the next run, or dies during a deploy.

entries.t: Dashboard and repo out of sync
entries.p: Compare infrastructure, hosting, cron, and environment settings declared in this repository against live configuration where read-only CLI or API access exists. Where dashboard state cannot be inspected from here, list the exact settings and dashboards I need to compare by hand. Flag drift that creates security, billing, or deploy risk.
entries.why: Finds where the hosting dashboard and the repo disagree.
entries.ev: Each declared setting (file:line) next to its live value (or "check in [named dashboard]"), highlighting every mismatch that affects uptime, security, or deploys.
entries.skip: Every hosting and database setting is managed purely from code with no manual dashboard overrides.
entries.tools: Vercel and database dashboards or MCP tools, read-only.
entries.line: Compares infrastructure settings declared in your code against what is actually configured in your hosting or cloud dashboards.

entries.t: Packages nobody uses, or that work by luck
entries.p: Audit declared dependencies for unused packages, undeclared imports satisfied only through transitive dependencies, and heavy libraries imported for trivial functionality. Check runtime code, config files (Next, Vite, PostCSS, Tailwind, ESLint), CLI scripts, and dynamic imports before calling any package unused.
entries.why: Finds packages nobody uses and packages that work only by accident.
entries.ev: Each flagged package with every reference found (including configs and scripts), its install or bundle cost, and whether removal or replacement is safe.
entries.skip: A tiny repo with only a handful of dependencies, or one that just finished a dependency cleanup.
entries.tools: Repository; a package checker such as knip or depcheck if already present.
entries.blind: Simple import scanners falsely flag packages loaded by build configs, PostCSS/Tailwind plugins, or CLI scripts. Verify those paths before recommending removal.
entries.line: Finds installed dependencies nothing uses anymore, imports working only by accident through another package, and huge libraries kept for one tiny helper.

entries.t: Old runtimes and when support ends
entries.p: Inventory actual versions and dependencies of Playwright, Puppeteer, system Chrome, Chromium caches and Electron apps. Verify current vendor-supported and security-fix thresholds rather than trusting hard-coded version numbers. Distinguish safe disposable caches from app-owned runtimes and report the rollback path before any cleanup.
entries.why: Finds old browser runtimes on your computer and which are safe to remove, before a cleanup breaks an app that needs them.
entries.ev: Each runtime with version, owner app, support status from the vendor, size, and a rollback path.
entries.skip: When browser tests are stable and disk space is fine.
entries.tools: A terminal on your computer; vendor release pages.
entries.blind: Do not delete shared runtimes or force a system Chrome until every dependent app is known.

entries.t: Did the agent actually finish this?
entries.line: Checks a completed feature or branch for classic coding-agent shortcuts: placeholder data, dead buttons, stubbed functions, skipped error states, and weakened tests.
entries.p: Audit the current branch (or the feature I name) for incomplete or faked implementation. Look for hardcoded or mock data left in real paths, stubbed or empty handlers, buttons or links wired to nothing, TODO/FIXME placeholders, swallowed errors (empty catch blocks), skipped or loosened tests, missing loading/empty/error states, and requirements from my request that were silently dropped. Check every changed file and trace each user action from the UI to storage and back.
entries.ev: A list of every shortcut, stub, dead control, weakened test, or dropped requirement with file:line and what a user would see if it shipped today, or a clear confirmation of every path you verified end to end.
entries.skip: A pure documentation change with no UI, logic, or test edits.
entries.blind: Agents skim for TODO comments and miss handlers that quietly return fake success or render static sample items. Trace the actual data flow for every new screen and action.
entries.why: Checks a completed feature or branch for classic coding-agent shortcuts: placeholder data, dead buttons, stubbed functions, skipped error states, and weakened tests.
entries.tools: Repository and its git history.

entries.line: Draws a plain-English map of your app — its screens, user roles, stored data, scheduled jobs, and outside services — so you can see how the pieces connect without reading code.
entries.p: Read the repository and build a plain-English map of how this product actually works today, written for the owner who directs changes and does not read code. Cover: (1) the main user roles and what each can see or do, (2) the key screens and how users move between them, (3) the core data records stored and how they relate, (4) every background job or scheduled task, (5) every external service or API the app depends on, and (6) where the highest-risk logic lives (payments, auth, writes, AI calls). Base every statement on the code and config files present today, ignoring outdated README descriptions.
entries.ev: A one-page plain-English system map covering those six areas, with key entry-point file paths listed underneath so I can point future sessions to the right folder.
entries.skip: A single-file script or a repo that already has an up-to-date plain-English architecture map verified against today's code.
entries.blind: Agents copy stale descriptions from README.md. Verify every screen, service, and table directly from source and config files, and flag any place the docs disagree with the code.
entries.why: Draws a plain-English map of your app — its screens, user roles, stored data, scheduled jobs, and outside services — so you can see how the pieces connect without reading code.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.p: Find where this application blurs the difference between missing, zero, unavailable, estimated, stale, and not applicable. Trace how each state is stored, how totals or averages handle it, and what appears on screen.
entries.why: Finds where 'we don't know' turns into 0 and then into a wrong total.
entries.ev: Each affected field (file:line), how absence is stored, how calculations treat it, what users see, and any chart or total it distorts.
entries.skip: Simple records with no optional numeric fields or aggregations.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only database access.
entries.line: Spots places where "unknown", "not loaded", or "not applicable" quietly turns into `0` and corrupts averages, charts, or totals.

entries.t: Where did this number come from?
entries.p: Trace each important derived number shown to users back to its raw source records, transformation logic, filters, and assumptions. Recompute a representative sample independently from raw inputs without relying on the existing calculation code to check itself. Flag discrepancies in definitions, units, dates, or source selection, and distinguish one-off errors from shared calculation bugs.
entries.why: Checks that every number on screen can be traced back to a source document.
entries.ev: For each key metric: its raw inputs, formula location (file:line), an independent recomputation on at least one real or sample record, and any disagreement ranked by impact.
entries.skip: Every displayed number is stored and shown verbatim with no calculation or aggregation.
entries.tools: Repository, read-only database, and the source documents the numbers come from.
entries.line: Traces every calculated number on screen back to its raw source records and recomputes an example independently to prove it is right.

entries.p: Find historical records whose meaning shifts when today's rules, categories, tax rates, plan limits, or schemas are applied retroactively. Check whether the system can still reproduce what a past record or report showed on an earlier date, distinguishing later source corrections from later rule changes. Recommend the smallest reliable fix without over-engineering full bitemporal storage unless truly required.
entries.why: Finds old records that read differently once today's rules are applied to them.
entries.ev: Each rule or classification that affects past records (file:line), which historical data predates it, concrete examples of how old records read today, and the smallest way to preserve historical accuracy.
entries.skip: An app with no historical reporting or evolving categories/pricing rules.
entries.tools: Read-only database access, history of database changes.
entries.line: Checks whether changing a rule, plan tier, or category today accidentally rewrites what historical records meant in the past.

entries.p: Audit every data import, CSV upload, and external sync for records that can be silently skipped, duplicated, overwritten, or linked to the wrong entity without raising an error. Check matching keys, conflict handling, partial failures, and summary logging.
entries.why: Finds rows that go missing or land on the wrong record during import, with no error.
entries.ev: Each import step (file:line) with its matching key, conflict rule, what gets logged on skip or mismatch, and whether counts-in are reconciled against counts-stored.
entries.skip: Apps where all data is entered one record at a time through forms, with no batch imports or syncs.
entries.tools: Repository, import logs, read-only database.
entries.line: Audits CSV uploads, syncs, and data imports for rows that get dropped, overwritten, duplicated, or attached to the wrong record without throwing an error.

entries.p: Identify where data relationships have greater analytical value than isolated fields. Find missing links, broken historical continuity, and relationships the source evidence cannot actually support.
entries.why: Finds links between records worth adding, and ones the evidence does not support.
entries.ev: Each relationship with its source evidence, current coverage, and gaps.
entries.skip: When the data layout is still changing weekly.
entries.tools: Read-only database access, source documents.

entries.p: Run a focused code-health audit calibrated to this repository's real conventions and operational risks. Every finding must cite a specific file:line, runnable command, trace, or commit; reject generic style preferences. Return a short ranked list of under fifteen repairable problems, each graded by confidence and user/maintenance impact.
entries.why: A general health check of the code that refuses findings without evidence.
entries.ev: Under fifteen ranked issues, each with file:line or a reproducible command, confidence, impact, and the smallest sensible fix.
entries.skip: You already have a specific symptom that fits a narrower investigation.
entries.tools: Repository access.
entries.line: Runs a disciplined codebase health check that drops style nitpicks and returns a short ranked list of concrete, repairable problems backed by proof.

entries.p: Compare every agent instruction and project doc file (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursorrules`, `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, and architecture notes) against the real directory layout, package scripts, and current code patterns. Flag stale rules referencing deleted files, replaced libraries, broken commands, or retired conventions.
entries.why: Finds instructions that send agents to files and patterns that no longer exist.
entries.ev: Each stale instruction with its file:line and the current repository fact it contradicts, plus the exact replacement or deletion proposed.
entries.skip: You have no agent instruction files yet, or you just audited and updated them.
entries.tools: Repository access.
entries.line: Checks `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursorrules`, and project docs against the actual repo to catch outdated paths, deleted commands, and dead patterns that mislead agents.

entries.p: Review the pending database migration or API schema change against the current live schema, previous release's queries, active background workers, and deployment sequence. Check whether it preserves existing data, causes table locks, breaks older client bundles or workers still draining during deploy (such as column renames, drops, or non-nullable additions), and whether a real rollback or recovery path exists. Never assume reverting app code alone rolls back a schema change.
entries.why: Checks that each database change works with the old code that is still live while a release finishes.
entries.ev: The migration diff (file:line), every query or consumer affected, how old and new app versions coexist during rollout, lock and rollback risks, and results from replaying the migration on a separate test copy if available.
entries.skip: The pending change touches no database schema, functions, policies, or shared API contracts.
entries.tools: Repository, migrations folder, previous release tag.
entries.line: Checks a pending database or API change to verify existing records survive, running users and old app versions don't break mid-deploy, and a real rollback path exists.
entries.avoid: Claiming rollback is safe solely because application code can be reverted.

entries.t: Walk me through what changed before I merge
entries.line: Explains an entire branch or pull request in plain English, flags edits outside your original request, and gives you a short manual test checklist you can click through yourself.
entries.p: Inspect the current branch diff against the default branch (or the pull request I name) and explain it for a product owner who does not read code. Group the changes by what a user or operator will experience, call out any file touched outside the stated goal, flag risky areas (data writes, permissions, billing, migrations, config changes, deleted checks), and write a five-minute manual click-test checklist I can run myself to verify the change works and did not break nearby flows.
entries.ev: A plain-English summary of user-visible and behind-the-scenes changes, a list of any out-of-scope edits with file paths, the top risks with file:line, and a numbered checklist of exact screens and actions for me to test.
entries.skip: A single-line wording fix or a branch with no changes against the default branch.
entries.blind: Agents summarize commit messages instead of reading the actual diff. Read the real diff line by line and flag anything the commits forgot to mention.
entries.why: Explains an entire branch or pull request in plain English, flags edits outside your original request, and gives you a short manual test checklist you can click through yourself.
entries.tools: Repository and its git history.

entries.t: Links, previews, and what Google sees
entries.line: Checks page titles, social share previews, favicons, 404/error pages, broken internal links, and search-engine settings before you share your site publicly.
entries.p: Audit this web application's public-facing metadata, share previews, error pages, and crawl settings. Check: page titles and meta descriptions across public routes (flag missing, duplicate, or placeholder defaults like "Create Next App"); Open Graph and Twitter/X preview tags and whether their image URLs resolve with absolute production URLs; favicon and app icons; custom 404 and 500 error pages; broken internal links or redirects; canonical URLs, sitemap, and robots.txt (flag accidental noindex tags or blocked public pages, as well as private or admin routes accidentally exposed to crawlers).
entries.ev: A table of public routes with title, description, share image status, and indexability, plus every missing icon, broken link, default error page, or robots/noindex problem with file:line.
entries.skip: A private internal tool or native-only app with no public web pages.
entries.blind: Relative share-image paths and staging noindex headers often pass local testing and break in production. Check how the base URL and environment flags resolve in production config.
entries.why: Checks page titles, social share previews, favicons, 404/error pages, broken internal links, and search-engine settings before you share your site publicly.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.p: Inspect API responses, Server Component props, SSR serialization payloads, and RPC returns sent from server to browser. Find places where full database rows or internal objects (internal flags, private emails, other tenants' IDs, tokens, audit metadata, or large unused blobs) are shipped to the client and merely left unrendered in the UI.
entries.why: Finds data sent to the browser that the screen hides but anyone can read.
entries.ev: Each over-exposed payload (file:line) showing the fields sent over the wire, the fields the screen actually uses, and every field that should stay on the server.
entries.skip: Static public pages with no server payloads or private user data.
entries.tools: Browser network panel or curl against a local server.
entries.line: Checks API responses and server-rendered page data for private database fields sent to the browser and merely hidden from view.

entries.t: When an outside service goes down
entries.p: Assume each external API, AI provider, or webhook source this product depends on hangs for 30 seconds, returns 429 or 503 for an hour, or delivers a burst of out-of-order webhooks when it recovers. Trace whether database transactions or connection pools stay held open during those calls, and whether core user flows degrade cleanly or lock up.
entries.why: Asks what happens to the app when an outside API, an AI provider or a service that sends it updates goes down.
entries.ev: Each external dependency with its timeout, retry behavior, resources held open while waiting, and what the user sees during an outage.
entries.skip: A self-contained app that makes no outbound API calls and receives no webhooks.
entries.tools: Repository; a local run with outside services made to fail on purpose.
entries.line: Maps what happens to your app when Stripe, an AI provider, email, or another third-party API hangs, rate-limits you, or goes offline.

entries.p: Trace every calculation involving money, percentages, basis points, quantities, weights, or rates across storage, API payloads, math helpers, and UI formatting. Flag binary floating-point arithmetic used where exact integer or decimal math is required, premature rounding that compounds across sums, and unclear unit conventions (such as cents versus dollars, or 0.05 versus 5.0 for 5%).
entries.why: Finds money and percentage values that change scale or lose precision along the way.
entries.ev: Each tracked value with its unit and numeric type at every layer (file:line), highlighting every hop where units shift or rounding loses accuracy.
entries.skip: Products that handle no money, rates, percentages, or converted units.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only access to the database layout.
entries.line: Catches pennies lost to floating-point math, percentages off by 100x (`0.05` vs `5`), and cents-versus-dollars mismatches across layers.

entries.t: Screens showing a change that was refused
entries.p: Trace every flow where the interface updates local state or cache optimistically before the server confirms the write. Show what happens to screen accuracy, queued actions, and error notices when the server rejects the request, times out, or returns different canonical values.
entries.why: Finds screens that show a change right away and keep showing it after the server refused it.
entries.ev: Each optimistic UI flow, what happens when the server rejects or drops the request, and a failing test or screenshot showing any unrolled-back state.
entries.skip: Every write waits for server confirmation before updating the screen.
entries.tools: In-app browser or Playwright set to block or alter requests.
entries.line: Checks features that update the screen immediately before the server responds, to see if rejected saves stay stuck on screen looking saved.

entries.p: List every animation and transition in this codebase with its duration, easing and animated properties. Count the distinct durations and the distinct easing curves. Find values used only once, transitions that name no property or no easing, and places that should share a value and do not. Propose the smallest set of shared durations and curves that covers what exists, and show which existing values map to which.
entries.why: Shows whether the app's motion follows a system or was typed one animation at a time.
entries.ev: A table of distinct durations and curves with counts, each outlier with file:line, and a mapping from existing values to a proposed set of about four durations and three curves.
entries.skip: Apps with a handful of animations, or a motion token file that everything already uses.
entries.tools: Repository access only.
entries.blind: Agents propose a token system and start migrating. Ask for the mapping only; migrating is a separate change.

entries.p: Find animations and transitions that trigger expensive layout or paint work per frame (animating width, height, top, left, margin, padding, heavy shadows or blurs, or driving styles from scroll/pointer events through React or component state). For the worst three candidates, record the interaction in a browser with CPU throttling enabled and report layout counts and dropped frames. Propose a cheaper alternative (such as transform or opacity) and note any visual tradeoff.
entries.why: Finds the animations that stutter on slower phones and laptops, and what each one costs.
entries.ev: Each expensive animation (file:line and animated property), plus throttled browser measurements (layout count and long frames) for the top three offenders before any code change.
entries.skip: Motion is limited to simple color, transform, or opacity transitions on small elements.
entries.tools: Repository; the app running locally and a browser with performance tooling (DevTools or Playwright).
entries.blind: Code search flags every height transition, including tiny accordions that cost almost nothing. Measure before recommending a rewrite.
entries.aka: Layout and paint cost of animation
entries.line: Finds animations that trigger expensive browser recalculations and stutter on phones or older laptops, backed by throttled performance recordings.

entries.p: Audit how this product behaves when the user's operating system requests reduced motion (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`). List every animation that translates, scales, rotates, or loops and check whether it has a reduced-motion fallback. Flag content that stays invisible if an entrance animation is skipped, auto-playing motion lasting over five seconds without a pause control, and drag/swipe gestures lacking a button or keyboard alternative. For each gap, specify the sensible reduced-motion replacement (usually a brief opacity fade or instant change).
entries.why: Finds motion that can make people dizzy or lock them out, and content that disappears when animation is turned off.
entries.ev: Every moving animation (file:line) and its reduced-motion handling, results from a browser check with reduced motion emulated showing anything that still moves or disappears, and the WCAG rule behind each gap (2.2.2, 2.3.1, 2.3.3, 2.5.1, or 2.5.7).
entries.skip: A personal prototype nobody else will use, or an app with zero movement animations.
entries.tools: Repository; a browser that can emulate prefers-reduced-motion.
entries.blind: Dropping one global CSS rule that sets all durations to 0ms can hide animated content or break state callbacks. Check what each real transition becomes.
entries.line: Checks how the app behaves when a user turns on "Reduce Motion" on their phone or computer, catching dizzying loops, trapped gestures, and content that fails to appear.

entries.t: Animations that restart, block or never finish
entries.p: Find animations and transitions that break when users act quickly instead of waiting for them to finish. Check for keyframe animations that restart abruptly on rapid triggers, exit animations skipped because elements unmount immediately, clicks or keyboard input blocked until a transition ends, focus shifting only after an animation completes, and end states that snap back to a different resting style. Reproduce up to three of the most reachable cases by re-triggering mid-animation, and propose the smallest fix for each.
entries.why: Finds motion that works in a demo and breaks under fast, real use.
entries.ev: Each broken case (file:line), the exact rapid-input sequence that triggers it, what the user sees (restart, jump, ignored click, or missing exit), and a reproduction for the worst one.
entries.skip: Apps whose only transitions are simple hover and focus color shifts.
entries.tools: Repository; the app running locally with a browser to trigger interactions quickly.
entries.line: Catches animations that look fine when clicked slowly and break under fast, impatient real-world clicking — restarting awkwardly, ignoring taps, or vanishing without exiting.

entries.p: Inventory every animation and transition in this product and state what concrete job it does for the user: confirming input, showing where an element came from or went, orienting navigation, indicating loading, or highlighting a state change. Flag every animation that conveys nothing or runs so frequently that it slows people down (menus, tooltips, keyboard-driven actions). Recommend remove, shorten, or keep for each with one sentence of reasoning. Do not propose adding new animations.
entries.why: Produces a list of animations to delete or shorten, which is usually the cheapest way to make an app feel faster.
entries.ev: A table with one row per animation: location (file:line), how often a user triggers it daily, the job it performs (or "none"), and remove, shorten, or keep.
entries.skip: An app with almost no motion — check "State changes with no feedback" instead.
entries.tools: Repository; the running app helps.
entries.blind: Do not defend decorative delays as "polish." If an animation teaches the user nothing and slows them down, mark it for removal or shortening.
entries.line: Audits every animation and lists the decorative or repetitive ones to delete or shorten so the interface feels snappier right away.

entries.p: Walk the product's main user flows and list up to ten moments where the interface changes with no visible feedback: a button press with no response, a deleted row vanishing abruptly, a panel appearing with no spatial cue, a multi-second wait with no loading indicator, or a save/error that happens silently. Exclude rapid, high-frequency actions users trigger dozens of times per minute. Rank the gaps by how much confusion each causes, and write a one-line motion spec (what changes, duration, and reduced-motion behavior) for each.
entries.why: Finds the few places where a small animation would remove real confusion.
entries.ev: Up to ten ranked moments with their user flow, component (file:line), what leaves the user guessing, and a one-line feedback spec.
entries.skip: You just finished a motion pass, or the complaint is that the app already moves too much (check "Motion with no job" instead).
entries.tools: Repository and the running app.
entries.blind: Do not suggest animating every state change. Limit the list to ten moments at most where missing feedback creates real user doubt.
entries.line: Finds the few high-impact moments where something saves, deletes, or shifts silently and leaves users wondering if their click worked.

entries.t: Make this database easier to trust and operate
entries.p:
Study how this PostgreSQL database actually works today — schema, relationships, data sources, reads, writes, background jobs, migrations, and consumers — using the live database state, repository, and operational evidence instead of documentation alone.

Identify the few root problems driving the most complexity, wasted work, data-quality risk, and operating cost. Focus on data correctness, reliable writes, duplicated logic, unused database objects, historical accuracy, and clarity for future maintenance.

Rank findings by measured impact. Separate confirmed problems from theoretical worries, and recommend changes that simplify the database instead of adding new infrastructure or recurring review processes.
entries.why: The broad starting point when the database feels hard to trust or costly, and you can't yet name one problem.
entries.ev: A short ranked list of confirmed problems, each with the tables, writers and consumers involved, the proof (query plans, samples, counts or a check against the source) and the smallest change that helps.
entries.skip: You already know the specific problem (go straight to the narrower prompt for it), or the project does not use PostgreSQL.
entries.avoid: Turning one look into a standing review, a new process, extra infrastructure or automated governance.
entries.tools: Needs: the repository and read-only database access. Helps: query statistics (pg_stat_statements) and, on Supabase, the built-in Advisors.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: database health, postgres health, simplify database, clean up database, healthier database, overall database review, supabase, neon, start here
entries.line: Runs one high-level check across a PostgreSQL database and ranks the handful of root issues causing most of the slowness, cost, or data-quality risk.

entries.t: Can we independently prove these numbers?
entries.p: Take a representative set of important figures from this database and independently reconstruct them from their original sources. Don't rely on the existing calculation code to verify itself. Find discrepancies in definitions, source selection, units, dates, classifications, and relationships. Determine which errors are isolated and which come from shared logic, then rank corrections by analytical impact.
entries.why: Important figures may be wrong even though their lineage is documented.
entries.ev: Samples from the original sources, an independent rebuild of each figure, each disagreement classified, how many records it affects, and the shared causes.
entries.skip: The figures are copied straight from the source with no calculation applied.
entries.avoid: Checking a value with the same code or source reading that produced it.
entries.tools: Needs: the repository, read-only database access and the original source documents.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: wrong numbers, incorrect numbers, inaccurate data, figures don't match, doesn't match the source, reconciliation, recompute, verify metrics, data provenance
entries.line: Rebuilds your most important figures from the original sources to prove whether the database has them right.

entries.t: Find data that is internally consistent but wrong
entries.p: Look for data in this PostgreSQL database that passes schema constraints and validation yet is analytically wrong. Test cross-table totals, accounting identities, historical continuity, plausible ranges, and expected source coverage. Separate real errors from intentional differences in reporting periods, granularity, or definitions.
entries.why: Every check passes, but totals or outputs still look implausible.
entries.ev: Cross-table reconciliations, identities and expected-population comparisons that fail, with example rows, source samples and how much data is affected.
entries.skip: There is no derived or analytical output, only records stored as entered.
entries.avoid: Calling different grains, as-of dates or reporting bases errors without checking their definitions.
entries.tools: Needs: the repository and read-only database access. Helps: pgTAP on a local or branch database, to turn confirmed rules into tests.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: totals are wrong, rows are valid but wrong, inaccurate data, sanity checks, reconciliation, implausible values, missing records
entries.line: Checks cross-table totals, accounting identities, and realistic ranges to catch data that passes every database rule yet is still factually wrong.

entries.t: Find where records silently change identity
entries.p: Trace how real-world entities are identified, matched, and linked across imports, source documents, and PostgreSQL tables. Find distinct entities merged by mistake, identical entities duplicated under separate IDs, and historical links that broke across updates. Identify the matching rule responsible and how many rows are affected before proposing fixes.
entries.why: Sources use aliases, changing identifiers, share classes or inconsistent names for the same thing.
entries.ev: Likely duplicates and false merges with their source IDs, the matching rule behind each, the records affected, a counterexample you can rerun and a query that surfaces the rest.
entries.skip: Every source shares one stable identifier and nothing is matched by name or fuzzy rules.
entries.avoid: Merging entities just because their names look alike.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only database access.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: duplicates, merged records, share classes merged, entity matching, wrong company, identity, dedupe
entries.line: Catches real-world entities (customers, companies, products) that got split into duplicate rows or accidentally merged into one across imports.

entries.t: Reproduce what the database believed in the past
entries.p: Choose important historical records and determine whether the system can reproduce what was known and reported at a specific past date, using the definitions and evidence available then. Distinguish later source corrections from later classification changes. Find where current logic silently rewrites historical meaning and recommend the smallest reliable solution.
entries.why: Past reports, backfills, restatements or changed classification rules matter.
entries.ev: Two or more past checkpoints, when each record was true and when it was known, the source revisions, and changes you can demonstrate.
entries.skip: Nobody needs past results to stay reproducible.
entries.avoid: Requiring bitemporal storage everywhere. Work out what is actually needed before choosing a structure.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only database access.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: historical report changed, old data meanings, as-of, restatement, backfill, point in time, history rewritten
entries.line: Checks whether you can still reproduce what the database said on an earlier date, after the data or the rules changed.

entries.t: Map every place that writes to the database
entries.p: Map every code path that creates, updates, or deletes rows in the core PostgreSQL tables: API endpoints, scripts, scheduled jobs, database functions, triggers, and automated agents. Show which writer owns each column, where writers overlap, and where two writers can overwrite or contradict each other. Recommend the simplest ownership model the current design supports.
entries.why: Several jobs, functions, APIs or agents change the same data, or nobody is sure who owns it.
entries.ev: A map from each writer to its tables and columns, then to triggers, side effects and consumers, with the cases where writers overlap or conflict.
entries.skip: One code path writes each table.
entries.avoid: Treating every extra writer as wrong. Find the paths that actually conflict or leave ownership unclear.
entries.tools: Repository and read-only database access.
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.
entries.tags: what writes to this table, mysterious overwrites, who owns this field, multiple writers, write ownership
entries.line: Lists every API route, script, trigger, background job, and agent that writes to your core tables, highlighting where two writers can collide.

entries.t: Stop rewriting data that hasn't changed
entries.p: Measure how much PostgreSQL write activity actually changes meaningful data. Look for repeated upserts rewriting identical rows, unnecessary delete-and-reinsert batches, needless index churn, and cascading refreshes. Identify writes that can be skipped safely without losing audit history, intentional last-seen timestamps, or recovery behavior.
entries.why: Upserts and updates run at high volume, imports are costly, or vacuum and write-ahead log churn look high.
entries.ev: Statement counts, the share of writes that really change a row, dead-row and churn figures, index and WAL effects where measurable, and before-and-after tests on a copy.
entries.skip: Write volume is small, or every write is a change that has to happen.
entries.avoid: Suppressing deliberate last-seen timestamps, trigger side effects, version counters or refreshes that are meant to happen.
entries.tools: Needs: the repository, read-only database access and a separate copy for before-and-after tests. Helps: query statistics (pg_stat_statements).
entries.plat: Any PostgreSQL host: Supabase, Neon, RDS, Cloud SQL or self-hosted.

entries.p: Give me the thorough, senior-level version of this task without expanding its scope. Look at what I'm trying to accomplish and identify what an experienced practitioner would check, question, or verify that I overlooked. Inspect the original code and data instead of relying on summaries. Name the specific checks or evidence that will prove the result is right, then refine the task plan accordingly. Keep the objective and scope tight, and skip extra process that adds complexity without improving the result.
entries.use: Use it before you hand an agent a task you only half know how to describe.
entries.line: Has the agent point out what a experienced engineer would check or verify that you left out, then tighten the plan without growing the scope.
entries.why: Has the agent point out what a experienced engineer would check or verify that you left out, then tighten the plan without growing the scope.

entries.p: Before we proceed, try to prove the proposed plan wrong. List the key assumptions it relies on, search the code, data, logs, and documentation for evidence against each one, and run the fastest check or test that could break it. Report which assumptions held, which failed, and which you could not check. If any failed, explain what changes and propose the smallest adjustment. Recommend going ahead only if nothing you found contradicts the plan.
entries.use: Use it when an agent's plan sounds right and you can't see why it might be wrong.
entries.line: Tells the agent to actively hunt for evidence that its own plan will fail before you approve it.
entries.why: Tells the agent to actively hunt for evidence that its own plan will fail before you approve it.

entries.p: Do not patch the visible symptom yet. Reproduce the problem first, then trace backward through code and data until you can explain in one or two plain sentences why it happens, citing the exact files, lines, or records involved. Search the codebase for every other place that shares the same cause. Report the cause, the proof, and every affected location. Then propose one fix that removes the underlying cause everywhere it applies, plus a check that fails if it returns. Wait for my yes before editing.
entries.use: Use it the second time the same kind of bug shows up.
entries.line: Stops the agent from patching symptoms; it must reproduce the bug, trace the exact cause, and find everywhere else that same cause lives.
entries.why: Stops the agent from patching symptoms; it must reproduce the bug, trace the exact cause, and find everywhere else that same cause lives.

entries.p: Before adding any new code, layer, setting, table, or dependency, look for something you can remove instead. Check whether deleting a redundant wrapper, special case, duplicate path, or unused rule solves the problem or makes it simpler. Only if removal cannot solve it, propose the smallest addition that works and justify each new piece. Judge options by how little there will be to understand and maintain next month, avoiding unnecessary moving parts.
entries.use: Use it when the proposed fix adds a new setting, table or service.
entries.line: Makes the agent try solving the problem by removing an existing layer, setting, or special case before adding anything new.
entries.why: Makes the agent try solving the problem by removing an existing layer, setting, or special case before adding anything new.

entries.p: Make the technical decisions yourself the way a senior engineer on this project would: follow the repository's existing patterns first, then established standards and official documentation, and inspect the codebase when unsure instead of asking me. Bring me only choices about product behavior, user impact, ongoing cost, or risks I must accept — each with your recommendation and how hard it is to change later. At the end, list the technical choices you made in one line each so I have a record.
entries.use: Use it when an agent keeps asking you technical questions you can't judge.
entries.line: Tells the agent to make routine technical decisions on its own and escalate only product, cost, or risk calls to you.
entries.why: Tells the agent to make routine technical decisions on its own and escalate only product, cost, or risk calls to you.

entries.p: Prove this works without relying only on the code or unit tests you just wrote. Pick an independent check that will actually fail if the fix is broken: walk through the running app like a real user, call the real endpoint, inspect the real stored data, compare against an outside source, or write a check from the original requirement without reading your implementation. Run that check, show the actual output, and state plainly what it still does not cover.
entries.use: Use it before you accept 'tests pass' as proof that something works.
entries.line: Requires the agent to prove a fix works using a path that cannot pass just because its own tests agree with its own code.
entries.why: Requires the agent to prove a fix works using a path that cannot pass just because its own tests agree with its own code.

Show me the short spec first and wait for my yes before editing files unless I already told you to proceed immediately.
