entries.use: Use it in the second session, after a read-only investigation found a real problem.
entries.line: Enforces a strict before-and-after loop: capture a failing case or baseline measurement first, apply the smallest fix, then rerun an independent check.
entries.why: Enforces a strict before-and-after loop: capture a failing case or baseline measurement first, apply the smallest fix, then rerun an independent check.

entries.p: Do not implement the first workable idea you think of. Lay out three meaningfully different ways to solve this: (1) the smallest conservative patch to the existing code, (2) the cleanest long-term design, and (3) a subtractive option that removes an existing layer, constraint, or special case. For each option, compare what else it could break, how easy it is to test, and how it fails. Recommend one in plain English and wait for my decision before editing anything.
entries.use: Use it for decisions that will be expensive to undo.
entries.line: Forces the agent to propose three distinct approaches (a minimal patch, a clean long-term fix, and a version that removes complexity) and recommend one before coding.
entries.why: Forces the agent to propose three distinct approaches (a minimal patch, a clean long-term fix, and a version that removes complexity) and recommend one before coding.

entries.p: Write a compact, self-contained technical handoff so a fresh agent session can resume this work cold. Include only: (1) verified facts and current system state, (2) approaches already tried and why they were ruled out, (3) exact files modified and any uncommitted changes in flight, and (4) the single next verifiable step. Record ground truth from the repository and commands run, skipping conversational recap.
entries.use: Use it before the agent compacts (shrinks its memory of the chat) or a long session ends. /pre-compact does the full version.
entries.line: Produces a compact, factual status note so a fresh agent session can resume right where this one stopped.
entries.why: Produces a compact, factual status note so a fresh agent session can resume right where this one stopped.

entries.p: Go past the first answer. For each claim you make, check the original evidence (the code, the data or the docs) and say which claims you verified and which you assumed. Then give one clear recommendation, the strongest argument against it, and the result that would change your mind.
entries.use: Add it to any prompt when you want depth and a firm recommendation, with the checking shown.
entries.line: Asks for a thorough answer that says what was checked and what was assumed, and ends with one firm recommendation.
entries.why: Asks for a thorough answer that says what was checked and what was assumed, and ends with one firm recommendation.

entries.p: Run a cleanup pass on the code touched by this branch or recent change. Look for logic duplicated in multiple places, functions whose callers need to know internal details, and thin pass-through wrappers that add indirection without value. Merge duplicates, put the core logic behind one clear entry point, and keep each interface simpler than the work inside it. Keep external behavior identical: run the existing tests before and after, and skip anything you cannot verify is safe. Summarize what you merged, moved, or deleted in plain English first, with file paths underneath.
entries.use: Use it as a cleanup pass on each pull request, or on a schedule for overdue maintenance. It pushes the agent to merge duplicated code, put core logic in one place and cut lines. Shared by Chris (@_khrus) on X on 7 Nov 2026; the idea is John Ousterhout's, from A Philosophy of Software Design, and Matt Pocock pointed him to it. /improve-codebase-architecture is the longer version: a scan, a report and an interview.
entries.line: Runs a focused cleanup pass over recently changed code to merge duplicated logic and hide messy internals behind one clear entry point.
entries.why: Runs a focused cleanup pass over recently changed code to merge duplicated logic and hide messy internals behind one clear entry point.

entries.line: Reads every claim your product makes in web pages, pricing tables, buttons, emails, and legal text, then checks whether the code actually keeps each promise.
entries.p: First read every user-facing promise in this repository: marketing and pricing copy, onboarding screens, button labels, confirmation and error messages, email templates, help text, and terms/privacy pages. A promise is anything a user could rely on (such as "cancel anytime", "we'll email you when ready", "saved automatically", "permanently deleted", "refunded within 5 days", or "private to your team"). Then trace the code and config responsible for keeping each promise on both normal paths and failure paths (failed payment, bounced email, crashed job, mobile browser). Classify each as Kept, Kept on happy path only, Not kept, or Unverifiable from repo (needs manual/dashboard check). Rank broken promises by trust or legal harm.
entries.ev: A table of promises listing where each is stated (file:line), where code enforces it (file:line or "nowhere"), its verdict, and for the top three broken ones a concrete scenario showing how a user notices.
entries.skip: An internal prototype with no public pages, user-facing emails, or billing.
entries.blind: Read the actual user-facing copy, email templates, and error strings before inspecting backend code — skipping copy misses the broken promises.
entries.why: Reads every claim your product makes in web pages, pricing tables, buttons, emails, and legal text, then checks whether the code actually keeps each promise.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.line: Reads your main user flows and predicts the confusing screens, vague error messages, and dead ends most likely to generate support emails.
entries.p: Walk this product's main user journeys in the code (sign-up, core workflow, billing, account settings, cancellation) and predict up to fifteen real support tickets users will send. Look only for issues grounded in existing code: dead-end error messages that give no next step, states with no escape hatch, buttons that silently do nothing, emails that contradict the screen, hidden limits, and intended behavior that looks broken. Write each ticket in a frustrated user's plain voice, cite the exact code behind it, and propose the smallest fix (often clearer wording, an empty state, or a confirmation). Stop once the real code-backed issues run out instead of padding to fifteen. Rank by how many users will hit each one.
entries.ev: Up to fifteen ranked tickets in user language, each tied to a specific screen, message, or state (file:line), expected frequency, and the smallest fix that prevents it.
entries.skip: A personal tool used only by you.
entries.blind: Never invent generic complaints like "the app feels slow." Every ticket must cite an actual message, missing state, or code path in this repository.
entries.why: Reads your main user flows and predicts the confusing screens, vague error messages, and dead ends most likely to generate support emails.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.t: How a clever user games you
entries.line: Finds loopholes an ordinary signed-in customer could exploit without hacking — infinite trials, stacked coupons, browser-only limits, or running up your AI/SMS bill.
entries.p: Think like a clever, opportunistic customer with a normal account and no hacking tools. Audit the code for ways they can get paid features for free or run up your bills: repeating free trials with fresh emails, reusing or stacking discount/referral codes, bypassing usage limits enforced only in browser code, timing upgrades/downgrades to dodge charges, keeping access after refunds or chargebacks, sharing accounts or abusing free invites, and triggering unbounded per-use costs (AI calls, SMS, emails, file storage, exports). For each loophole, give the exact user steps, whether the server enforces the rule today, a rough monthly cost if 100 users did it, and whether fixing it is a small code change or a pricing/product policy call.
entries.ev: Each abuse path with reproduction steps, current enforcement (file:line or "missing"), rough cost at 100 abusive users, and whether it needs code or a product decision.
entries.skip: A completely free app with no usage caps and no metered per-action costs.
entries.blind: Stay focused on business-logic and billing loopholes ordinary users can trigger — classic security vulnerabilities like SQL injection belong in the Security checks.
entries.why: Finds loopholes an ordinary signed-in customer could exploit without hacking — infinite trials, stacked coupons, browser-only limits, or running up your AI/SMS bill.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.line: Finds unlinked pages, untouched settings, stale feature flags, and dead integrations that cost maintenance while helping almost nobody.
entries.p: Identify features, screens, settings, feature flags, integrations, legacy plan tiers, export formats, or unfinished experiments that could be deleted with minimal user impact. Use whatever real evidence is accessible — routes with no navigation links, analytics events, database row counts, logs, flag config, and git history. For each candidate, assess its upkeep cost (code, tests, dependencies, support burden), the evidence it is unused, who could still reach it (including direct URLs, email links, bookmarks, or cron jobs), and what removal takes. Recommend the top three cuts with the best maintenance-saved-to-risk ratio.
entries.ev: A ranked list of deletion candidates with usage evidence (query, count, or analytics check — marking anything that requires your live analytics dashboard), upkeep cost, potential impact, and the top three to remove first.
entries.skip: A brand-new product under a few months old with no real user history yet.
entries.blind: Code with zero internal callers can still be hit via bookmarked URLs, email links, webhooks, or scheduled jobs. Check every entry point before calling a feature dead.
entries.why: Finds unlinked pages, untouched settings, stale feature flags, and dead integrations that cost maintenance while helping almost nobody.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.line: Traces a single customer payment from checkout through webhooks, database rows, access grants, receipts, refunds, and chargebacks to spot where money or access goes wrong.
entries.p: Trace a single dollar from the moment a customer pays through every system that records or reacts to it: checkout, payment provider, webhooks, database records, feature access grants, receipts/emails, and revenue reporting. Then trace the unhappy paths: declined card, payment retry, duplicate webhook, out-of-order webhook (arriving before the user or checkout row exists), partial refund, full refund, chargeback, mid-cycle plan change, cancellation, and non-default currency. At each step, identify the source of truth, what happens on failure or retry, and where your records or user access can fall out of sync with the payment provider.
entries.ev: A step-by-step trace of the happy path and each unhappy path with handler locations (file:line), source of truth per step, and every gap where money can be double-counted, lost, or mismatched against granted access.
entries.skip: A product that takes no payments, or links out to a hosted payment page and stores zero payment state.
entries.blind: Do not stop after tracing successful checkouts. Duplicate and out-of-order webhooks plus refunds and chargebacks are where real billing bugs hide.
entries.why: Traces a single customer payment from checkout through webhooks, database rows, access grants, receipts, refunds, and chargebacks to spot where money or access goes wrong.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.line: Calculates what each additional active user costs you across hosting, AI models, email, storage, and APIs, and flags features whose cost outruns your subscription price.
entries.p: Calculate the marginal monthly cost of adding one typical active customer. List every paid service this product uses (hosting, functions, database, file storage, bandwidth, AI models, email, SMS, search, error tracking, third-party APIs) and trace from code what user actions trigger charges. Estimate monthly usage per active customer using logs or database stats where available, stating assumptions clearly where not. Compare total per-user cost against each pricing tier, and highlight features whose cost scales faster than revenue (such as unthrottled AI calls, full-size image uploads, or unlimited free-tier exports). Fetch current published vendor prices if you have web access and cite the URL; if you cannot verify live pricing, mark every price clearly as an estimate for me to confirm on the vendor's pricing page.
entries.ev: A cost-per-user breakdown by service and feature with triggering code (file:line), stated assumptions, verified vs. estimated prices, margin per plan, and the two or three features that hurt most at 10x users.
entries.skip: A flat-fee static product with zero metered services and no paid plans.
entries.blind: Never present memorized pricing as confirmed fact. Cite a live pricing source or mark the number as an unverified estimate.
entries.why: Calculates what each additional active user costs you across hosting, AI models, email, storage, and APIs, and flags features whose cost outruns your subscription price.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: If a vendor doubles its price or disappears
entries.line: Shows how tightly your app is wired to each outside vendor, how hard it would be to leave on 30 days' notice, and one cheap safeguard for the top two risks.
entries.p: Map this product's dependence on every external vendor, platform, or API (hosting, database, auth, payments, email, AI providers, app stores, analytics, and third-party SDKs). For each, measure how deeply it is embedded: how many files import or call it directly, whether one internal wrapper isolates it, whether your data can be cleanly exported, and which core features stop without it. Stress-test three scenarios for each vendor: price doubles, terms ban your use case, or it shuts down with 30 days' notice. Rank vendors by potential damage and suggest one cheap hedge for the top two without proposing a migration today.
entries.ev: A vendor table listing file touch count, single wrapper (yes/no), data exportability, features lost on outage, estimated switch effort, and one low-cost hedge for each of the top two risks.
entries.skip: A small project using only one or two standard services already isolated behind clean wrappers.
entries.blind: Do not recommend migrating off vendors immediately. Give a clear risk picture and small, practical hedges.
entries.why: Shows how tightly your app is wired to each outside vendor, how hard it would be to leave on 30 days' notice, and one cheap safeguard for the top two risks.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: Emails and messages people actually receive
entries.line: Audits every email, text, or notification your app sends for broken links, placeholder wording, wrong sender details, double sends, and silent delivery failures.
entries.p: Find every email, SMS, push notification, or in-app message this application sends. For each one, read the actual template and trigger code and check: what triggers it, whether retries or webhooks can send it twice, whether links inside it could point to localhost or a broken URL in production, what sender name and reply-to address it uses, whether marketing or digest messages include a working unsubscribe link, whether placeholder or embarrassing wording remains, and what happens when the email or SMS provider rejects or bounces it.
entries.ev: A list of every outgoing message with its trigger (file:line), template path, link and wording issues, retry/duplicate risk, and a short checklist of DNS or provider dashboard checks (such as SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or verified sender domain) that cannot be verified from the repo.
entries.skip: An app that sends no emails, texts, or notifications.
entries.blind: Agents check that a send function exists and skip reading the actual subject line, body text, and link URL builder. Inspect the rendered text and URL construction for every template.
entries.why: Audits every email, text, or notification your app sends for broken links, placeholder wording, wrong sender details, double sends, and silent delivery failures.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: Build it, buy it, or skip it?
entries.line: Before you ask an agent to build a big feature from scratch, checks whether an existing tool, a simpler manual step, or skipping it makes more sense for a solo builder.
entries.p: Before we build the feature I am describing, evaluate three paths for a solo builder who wants low ongoing maintenance: (1) build it inside this codebase, (2) use an established service or library that already fits our stack, or (3) ship a much simpler or manual version first until usage proves it needs software. Inspect the repository first so your comparison reflects our actual stack, existing dependencies, and hosting limits. For each option, compare upfront work, ongoing maintenance and edge cases I will own forever (security, compliance, retries, deliverability, edge cases), vendor lock-in, and rough cost. Recommend one option and state what would change your mind.
entries.ev: A plain-English comparison of the three options grounded in this repo's stack (citing package.json or equivalent config), the hidden maintenance traps of building it ourselves, and one clear recommendation.
entries.skip: A tiny feature unique to this product's core value where no off-the-shelf tool applies.
entries.blind: Coding agents default to "we can build this easily" because writing the first version is fast while owning edge cases for two years is invisible. Price the two-year maintenance burden up front.
entries.why: Before you ask an agent to build a big feature from scratch, checks whether an existing tool, a simpler manual step, or skipping it makes more sense for a solo builder.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.line: Audits every runtime AI model call inside your app for prompt-injection traps, runaway costs, retired models, missing output checks, and silent slowdowns.
entries.p: Audit every place this application calls an AI model at runtime. For each call check: (1) model ID and whether it is deprecated or nearing retirement, (2) what untrusted input enters the prompt (user text, scraped pages, uploaded files, emails) and its prompt-injection exposure, (3) what the model's output can trigger (display text, tool calls, database writes, emails, charges), (4) timeouts, retries, and fallback behavior when the provider is slow or down, (5) schema/length/allowlist validation on outputs before use, (6) cost per call and calls triggered per user action, (7) whether personal user data is sent to the model provider, and (8) whether any eval or test detects answer quality dropping. Rank findings by severity: unauthorized actions first, cost blowups second, silent quality degradation third.
entries.ev: Every runtime model call (file:line) with model ID, untrusted inputs, downstream actions triggered by output, timeout/fallback, output validation, estimated calls per action, and ranked risks.
entries.skip: An application that makes zero AI API calls at runtime.
entries.blind: Do not stop at reading the prompt string. Trace where the model's response actually flows and what actions it can execute.
entries.why: Audits every runtime AI model call inside your app for prompt-injection traps, runaway costs, retired models, missing output checks, and silent slowdowns.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.t: Things that break on a date
entries.line: Builds a timeline of everything set to expire or fail automatically — certificates, API keys, app store renewals, startup credits, retiring model versions, and hardcoded dates.
entries.p: Find everything in this project that will break on a future calendar date without any code change. Check: TLS certificates and signing keys, expiring API tokens and OAuth secrets, app store certificates and OAuth verification renewals, domain renewals, free-tier or startup credits expiring, retiring vendor APIs/SDKs/AI model IDs referenced in code, hardcoded years or date cutoffs, scheduled jobs with end dates, and growing counters or storage quotas nearing limits. Put everything on one timeline, soonest first, stating how you found each date and whether any automated alert warns ahead of time. Separate dates verified from code/config from dates you cannot see that I must check in a named dashboard.
entries.ev: One chronological risk timeline listing each item, verified date (or "check in [named dashboard]"), evidence (file:line or command), what breaks when it hits, and whether any advance warning exists.
entries.skip: A brand-new local prototype with no deployed domain, external API keys, or scheduled jobs.
entries.blind: Never guess expiry dates you cannot inspect. Mark every dashboard-only renewal clearly for manual verification.
entries.why: Builds a timeline of everything set to expire or fail automatically — certificates, API keys, app store renewals, startup credits, retiring model versions, and hardcoded dates.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: How you'd find out it's broken
entries.line: Checks your core user flows one by one to show which outages would alert you within minutes and which you'd only learn about from an angry user.
entries.p: List the five to ten critical jobs this product must keep working (sign-in, checkout, outgoing emails, core data reads/writes, nightly jobs, imports). For each one, answer directly: if it stopped working at 2am, how would I find out and how long would it take? Inspect only what actually exists in code and config — error trackers, alerting rules, uptime checks, health endpoints, failed-payment hooks, and swallowed exceptions — and flag external alerting dashboards you cannot inspect from the repo. Classify each flow as: alerts within minutes, noticed within a day, or only discovered when a user complains. For each blind spot, propose the single smallest signal that catches it (one alert, one heartbeat check, or one daily count check).
entries.ev: A table of critical flows showing current detection (file:line, dashboard to verify, or "none"), expected delay before you notice, and one lightweight alert for each gap.
entries.skip: A pre-launch prototype with no external users yet.
entries.blind: Writing to a log file nobody alerts on does not count as monitoring. Check who actually gets notified and how.
entries.why: Checks your core user flows one by one to show which outages would alert you within minutes and which you'd only learn about from an angry user.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.line: Exposes invisible framework and hosting defaults your app runs on — session lifetimes, upload limits, timeouts, cache lengths, rate limits, and email headers — and flags the risky ones.
entries.p: Audit settings left at their framework, library, or hosting defaults that materially affect users, security, or cost: session duration and idle logout, password and reset-token expiry, upload size caps, request timeouts, cache headers, rate limits, retry counts, default time zone/locale/currency, pagination sizes, email sender and reply-to, image storage settings, log retention, backup schedules, data region, and hard vs. soft deletes. Report only defaults that could plausibly hurt this product. Verify each default value against the installed version's source code in `node_modules` (or equivalent lockfile/package source) or official docs; mark anything you could not verify locally as unconfirmed.
entries.ev: A focused list of risky defaults showing the setting, current value and where you confirmed it (file:line, installed package source, or doc reference), plain-English user impact, and a suggested explicit value.
entries.skip: Every major runtime, auth, upload, timeout, and retention setting is already explicitly configured in one documented config file.
entries.blind: Framework defaults change between major versions. Verify against the exact version installed instead of quoting from memory.
entries.why: Exposes invisible framework and hosting defaults your app runs on — session lifetimes, upload limits, timeouts, cache lengths, rate limits, and email headers — and flags the risky ones.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.t: Where people's personal data ends up
entries.line: Tracks every piece of personal information you collect across databases, logs, error trackers, analytics, emails, and AI calls, and checks what it takes to delete a user completely.
entries.p: Trace all personal user data from collection (forms, sign-up, billing, uploads, analytics, IP/device metadata, support tools) to every destination it reaches: database tables, file buckets, server logs, error trackers, session recordings, analytics, email/CRM tools, AI API calls, exports, and backups. For each destination, note retention, access scope, and whether data leaves to a third party (flagging external tool settings that need manual dashboard checks). Then trace a real account-deletion request: list every place user data would need to be removed from and whether code handles it today. Highlight sensitive data logged in plain text, unused fields still being collected, and any mismatch with your privacy page.
entries.ev: A map from each collected personal field to every storage/external destination (file:line), a deletion checklist separating automated cleanup from manual steps, and any mismatch with the privacy page.
entries.skip: A local or anonymous tool with zero accounts, forms, analytics, or personal data.
entries.blind: Check server logs, error trackers, and analytics calls first — personal data leaks there far more often than in primary database tables.
entries.why: Tracks every piece of personal information you collect across databases, logs, error trackers, analytics, emails, and AI calls, and checks what it takes to delete a user completely.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: Things you may not be allowed to ship
entries.line: Checks fonts, icons, images, third-party packages, and copied snippets for licenses that restrict commercial use or require attribution.
entries.p: Audit everything shipped in this project for licensing or usage restrictions: package licenses in lockfiles (especially copyleft licenses like GPL/AGPL in closed-source products, or non-commercial/source-available licenses in paid apps), code snippets copied without attribution, web/app font files and their license terms, images/icons/illustrations/audio in asset folders, third-party logos or brand assets, AI-generated media whose source tool has commercial terms, and scraped or external datasets. For each flagged item, state the license or provenance found, whether this usage fits, and the next step (attribute, replace, purchase a license, or verify). Flag uncertain items for human or legal review without giving legal advice.
entries.ev: Every asset or package with a potential license issue (file path and where the license was found), whether current use fits, and the concrete action needed, separating clear fixes from items needing human confirmation.
entries.skip: A private personal script nobody else will see, download, or pay for.
entries.blind: Do not stop after scanning `package.json`. Fonts, icon packs, downloaded images, and pasted code snippets in asset/source folders are where real license problems usually hide.
entries.why: Checks fonts, icons, images, third-party packages, and copied snippets for licenses that restrict commercial use or require attribution.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.line: Finds every account, dashboard setting, manual habit, and secret that lives only in your head or on your computer, and drafts a one-page emergency runbook.
entries.p: Imagine I became unreachable tomorrow and a capable developer had to keep this product running using only this repository. Identify everything missing from the repo: external accounts and billing ownership (hosting, domain, database, payments, email, app stores), dashboard-only secrets and settings, manual recurring work (deploys, renewals, exports, support replies, data fixes), external cron jobs, undocumented code quirks, and anything tied to my personal machine. For each gap, note what breaks and how soon, plus the smallest fix (a repo doc, script, shared password vault entry, or backup owner). Format the actionable output as a clean one-page emergency runbook naming where each secret lives (names only, never values).
entries.ev: Single points of failure ranked by how quickly each breaks, a draft one-page runbook covering accounts, deploys, manual tasks, and secret locations (names only, never secret values), and a short list of account-ownership questions only I can fill in.
entries.skip: A disposable weekend experiment with no external accounts, users, or ongoing operations.
entries.blind: Never read, print, or copy secret values into the runbook. Record only variable names and which dashboard or password manager holds them.
entries.why: Finds every account, dashboard setting, manual habit, and secret that lives only in your head or on your computer, and drafts a one-page emergency runbook.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.t: What agents keep getting wrong here
entries.line: Mines your git history for reverts and fix-on-fix commits to spot mistakes coding agents keep repeating, and drafts exact lines for `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` to prevent them.
entries.p: Analyze this repository's git history to uncover mistakes coding agents keep repeating. Look for reverts, rapid follow-up fix commits, files that repeatedly change together yet live far apart, and edits to generated files or broken conventions. Group recurring mistakes by root cause (undocumented rule, generated file, required rebuild step, misleading name, synced pair of files, broken local test). For each recurring cause, cite two or three commit hashes as proof and draft one or two crisp lines for `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` — or an automated check — that would have prevented it. Skip anything already clearly documented.
entries.ev: Recurring causes ranked by frequency, supporting commit hashes, and exact proposed additions or edits for your instruction file (marked New or Replaces).
entries.skip: A new repository with fewer than roughly fifty commits of history.
entries.blind: Reject vague platitudes like "write clean tests." Every proposed rule must trace directly to real commits in this repository.
entries.why: Mines your git history for reverts and fix-on-fix commits to spot mistakes coding agents keep repeating, and drafts exact lines for `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` to prevent them.
entries.tools: Repository and its git history.

entries.line: Writes a grounded, hour-by-hour preview of the most likely serious outage, data loss, security leak, or surprise bill waiting in your current setup — and the one fix worth doing this week.
entries.p: From the actual code, config, deploy setup, data model, and third-party dependencies in this repository, identify the three likeliest ways this product suffers its first serious incident: data loss or corruption, prolonged outage, security/privacy leak, or a surprise usage bill. Take the #1 likeliest scenario and write a grounded pre-mortem incident report: exact trigger, hour-by-hour timeline, how you find out, what compounds the damage, what gets lost, recovery time, and impact. Every single step in the timeline must cite a real file, setting, or missing safeguard in this repo (or explicitly flag a dashboard setting to check). End with three preventive fixes ordered by effort, naming the single one worth doing this week.
entries.ev: Three ranked incident risks with triggers, one evidence-backed incident timeline citing real files/settings at every step, and three preventive fixes with effort estimates.
entries.skip: A throwaway prototype with no users, no stored data worth keeping, and no metered billing.
entries.blind: Do not write dramatic fiction. Every link in the incident chain must be possible under this repository's actual code and configuration.
entries.why: Writes a grounded, hour-by-hour preview of the most likely serious outage, data loss, security leak, or surprise bill waiting in your current setup — and the one fix worth doing this week.
entries.tools: Repository access.

entries.t: Can you get your data back if something goes wrong?
entries.line: Checks whether your database, uploaded files, and user content are actually backed up and restorable — whatever database or host you use.
entries.p: Audit how this product protects against accidental data loss across every store it uses (SQLite, Postgres, Supabase, Firebase, Convex, cloud file storage, or external SaaS data). From the repository, infrastructure config, and scripts, trace: what destructive operations exist in code or admin tools (hard deletes, cascades, overwrites, migration drops), whether soft-delete or undo exists for user-triggered deletions, what backup or point-in-time recovery settings are declared in config, and what data lives in places with no backup configured. Clearly separate what you verified in the repository from backup settings that live only in a hosting dashboard and require my check.
entries.ev: Every data store and file bucket found (file:line), the destructive paths that can wipe data permanently, what backup/restore mechanism is visible in config, and a short checklist of dashboard settings I must confirm and one safe restore drill to run.
entries.skip: A stateless tool or static site that stores no user data or uploaded files.
entries.blind: Agents assume a managed database host includes tested backups by default. Free tiers often have no point-in-time recovery or short retention, and file buckets (avatars, uploads) are frequently unbacked-up even when the database is. Flag every assumption that needs dashboard verification.
entries.why: Checks whether your database, uploaded files, and user content are actually backed up and restorable — whatever database or host you use.
entries.tools: Repository access. Some answers need your hosting, billing or vendor dashboards; the report names them.

entries.line: Forces the agent to label every claim as Checked, Inferred, or Guessed so you can tell verified facts from confident assumptions.
entries.use: Use it when you can't tell whether an agent actually looked or only sounds sure, especially before acting on what it says.
entries.p: Separate what you verified from what you assumed. In your answer, tag every factual claim as Checked (you ran it, read the file, or measured it — state how), Inferred (it follows from something you checked — state what), or Guessed (unverified). Before replying, verify any Guessed claim that your recommendation depends on. List any remaining guesses clearly along with what would change if they turned out wrong. Never state a guess in the same confident tone as a checked fact.
entries.why: Forces the agent to label every claim as Checked, Inferred, or Guessed so you can tell verified facts from confident assumptions.

entries.why: Makes the agent imagine the shipped change has already gone wrong, list the likeliest causes specific to your project, and add safeguards before editing.

entries.line: Wraps up a completed task with a short plain-English explanation of what changed, what could go wrong, and how to test it yourself, plus two quick check-in questions.
entries.use: Use it on any change you'll have to live with, especially when you don't read the code yourself.
entries.p: When you finish, explain what you changed so I could describe it to someone else and spot trouble later. Assume I understand the product and do not read code. entries.why: Wraps up a completed task with a short plain-English explanation of what changed, what could go wrong, and how to test it yourself, plus two quick check-in questions.

entries.line: Maps everyone and everything affected by a change beyond the code — active users, saved bookmarks, emails already sent, search engines, cached copies, and connected services — and plans the transitions.

entries.p: Before making this change, list everyone and everything that will feel its impact beyond the files you edit: users on each plan, people mid-task during deploy, saved links and bookmarks, links inside emails already sent, search engines, analytics and reports, external apps or scripts calling this, cached responses, older client or app versions still running, in-flight background jobs, and admins or support. entries.why: Maps everyone and everything affected by a change beyond the code — active users, saved bookmarks, emails already sent, search engines, cached copies, and connected services — and plans the transitions.

areaBlurb.Architecture and hidden complexity: Spots where the way the code is built invites bugs: status spread across many places, words that change meaning between layers, and layers that cost more than they help.
areaBlurb.Performance and scale: Where time and money go as the data grows. Every claim here needs a measurement before and after.
areaBlurb.Correctness and reliability: What happens when something runs twice, fails, times out or happens in the wrong order, and whether people can tell a stand-in value from the real one.
areaBlurb.Testing and security: What the tests really prove, and where input from outside can reach something sensitive.
areaBlurb.Infrastructure and environment: The path from a merged change to the live site, what automated checks cost, and the computer the agents run on.
areaBlurb.Data integrity and analytics: Telling missing from zero, knowing where each number came from, and records whose meaning changes over time.
areaBlurb.Agent harness and modern stack: Newer kinds of trouble: out-of-date agent instructions, old and new versions running at once after a deploy, data leaking into pages, outside services going down, rounding errors, and screens that show a change before it is saved.
areaBlurb.Start here: One broad look when the database feels hard to trust or costly. If you can already name the problem, skip it and pick the narrower prompt.
areaBlurb.Accuracy and evidence: Proves the data is right, not just valid: rebuilt figures, whole populations, stable identities and past results that still reproduce.
areaBlurb.Writes and ingestion: Who writes what, how often it changes nothing, and whether imports survive retries and corrections.
areaBlurb.Schema and dependencies: Fewer objects, one home for each fact, and a model a new engineer or agent can read.
areaBlurb.Performance and maintenance: Where storage, time and write cost actually go, and what grows expensive first. Every claim needs a measurement.
areaBlurb.Rebuild and safe change: Changes and restores proved on a separate database before anyone relies on them.
areaBlurb.Agent decisions: Turns questions agents keep asking you into rules they can apply themselves.
areaBlurb.Workflows: Short routes through the database prompts for a whole job. Start with the first step and only take the optional ones when the evidence points there.
areaBlurb.Motion: How the interface moves: whether animation follows a system, what it costs, who it leaves out, and where it helps or gets in the way. Each prompt works in any agent. The motion-kit plugin's /motion runs the same checks with frame-by-frame captures.

supabase: Official skills for Supabase and Postgres work. Install with: claude plugin marketplace add supabase/agent-skills, then claude plugin install supabase@supabase-agent-skills. Other agents: npx skills add supabase/agent-skills.
bestpractices: Rules for queries, indexes, connections, locking and RLS. Works on any Postgres, not only Supabase. Install with: claude plugin install postgres-best-practices@supabase-agent-skills.
pgss: Postgres extension that counts how often each statement runs and how long it takes. Check it is enabled before trusting its numbers.
advisors: Built-in security and performance checks in the Supabase dashboard. Read their output rather than running another scanner.
hypopg: Tests whether an index would help without building it. Optional, and not needed for most investigations.
pgtap: SQL tests for rules and RLS policies. Run them on a local or branch database, never production.
declarative: Keep the desired schema in files and generate migrations from it. Weigh it against the migration workflow you already have.
pgdocs: The reference for exact behaviour. Check the version your database runs.

recipes.line: Traces the real root cause, locks in a failing reproduction first, applies one narrow fix after you approve, verifies it independently, and explains what changed in plain English.
recipes.when: A stubborn or recurring bug keeps resisting quick patches.
steps: trace the real cause and everywhere else it applies without editing app code
write a minimal test or reproduction script that fails today
fix the confirmed root cause after you approve
verify the fix via a real-world path separate from your own unit test
get a short plain-English summary and two understanding checks
recipes.copy:
A bug you can't explain. Trace the root cause, prove it with a failing check, apply the narrowest fix, verify independently, and explain what changed.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step before moving on. Do not edit application code during Steps 1, 2, 4, or 5.

Step 1 (root cause — read-only): Do not patch the visible symptom yet. Reproduce the bug, trace backward through code and data until you can explain in one or two plain sentences why it happens (with exact file:line or records), and find every other place sharing that cause. Propose one fix that removes the cause everywhere it applies. Wait for my yes.

Step 2 (reproduction — no app edits): Add one minimal failing test or reproduction script that reliably demonstrates the bug today. Do not change application code yet. Show the failing output and wait for my yes.

Step 3 (narrow fix): Implement the smallest fix that removes the proven root cause and makes Step 2's check pass. Do not refactor unrelated code. Wait for my yes.

Step 4 (independent verification): Prove the fix works without relying only on the code or test you just wrote. Exercise the real flow (browser click-through, real endpoint, or real stored data), show the result, and state plainly what it still does not cover.

Step 5 (plain-English wrap-up): In under 250 words for someone who knows the product and does not read code, cover what went wrong, what you changed and why, what users will see, what could still go wrong and how I'd spot it, and one thing I can check myself. End with two short questions to confirm I understood the key parts.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Measures where seconds actually go, narrows down waiting chains or repeated work, fixes only the #1 measured bottleneck, and re-measures to prove the speedup.
recipes.when: A screen or workflow feels sluggish and you want measured improvements instead of guesswork.
steps: time the slowest user flows from click to database (read-only)
check whether independent steps are waiting sequentially (read-only, run if Step 1 shows waterfalls)
check for identical work running repeatedly (read-only, run if Step 1 shows repeated queries/renders)
wait for approval, then make one targeted fix
rerun the exact Step 1 measurement and verify nothing broke
recipes.copy:
It got slow. Measure where the time goes, fix only the single biggest measured bottleneck, and prove the speedup with before-and-after numbers.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay strictly read-only during Steps 1, 2, 3, and 5 — do not edit code, data, or config until I approve Step 4.

Step 1 (measure end to end — read-only): Trace and measure the slowest user journey(s) from browser click to database response, identifying round trips, waterfalls, slow queries, repeated work, blocking synchronous handlers, or large loops. Bring back: a measured timing breakdown showing each step's share of total latency (file:line). If everything is already fast and costs are flat, say so and stop. Watch out: require real measurements, never guesses from static reading.

Step 2 (waiting chains — read-only, skip if Step 1 showed no sequential waits): Inspect the slow path for independent async steps waiting sequentially, and check shared transactions, pool sizes, and API rate limits before recommending parallelism. Bring back: each sequential chain (file:line), its measured time, and constraints to respect.

Step 3 (repeated work — read-only, skip if Step 1 showed no duplicate work): Inspect the slow path for expensive operations repeated with unchanged inputs. Bring back: each repeated call (file:line), frequency, measured cost, and exact cache-invalidation rules if caching is proposed.

Step 4 (fix the #1 bottleneck): After I approve, apply only the smallest fix targeting the single largest measured cost from Steps 1–3.

Step 5 (prove the speedup): Rerun the exact measurement method from Step 1 on realistic input and report exact before-and-after timings alongside an independent check that behavior stayed identical. If the speedup cannot be measured, state what evidence is missing instead of claiming a win.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Traces a suspect figure to its raw inputs, checks whether missing values turned into zero or units drifted, fixes only confirmed bugs, and verifies independently.
recipes.when: A balance, metric, chart, or total on screen disagrees with what you expect.
steps: trace the metric to raw inputs and recompute one example (read-only)
check whether unknown or missing values are counted as zero (read-only)
check cents vs. dollars, percentages, and float rounding (read-only)
wait for approval, then fix only proven bugs
recompute again against raw source records to confirm the fix
recipes.copy:
The numbers look wrong. Trace a suspect number to its source, check missing-as-zero and unit/rounding bugs, fix only proven causes, and verify independently.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay strictly read-only during Steps 1, 2, 3, and 5 — do not edit code, data, or config until I approve Step 4.

Step 1 (source trace — read-only): Trace the suspect metric(s) to raw inputs, transformation logic, filters, and assumptions, and recompute at least one real example independently. Bring back: raw inputs, formula (file:line), and independent recomputation. Stop if displayed numbers are stored verbatim with no calculation.

Step 2 (missing vs zero — read-only): Check where missing, unavailable, stale, or not-applicable values turn into 0 in storage, calculations, or display. Bring back: each affected field (file:line), how absence is stored, how math treats it, and what users see. Stop if no optional numeric fields are involved.

Step 3 (rounding and units — read-only): Trace currency, percentages, and rates across storage, API, and UI for floating-point drift, premature rounding, or scale mismatches (0.05 vs 5.0, cents vs dollars). Bring back: each value's numeric type and unit at every hop (file:line). Stop if no money, rates, or conversions are involved.

Step 4 (fix confirmed causes): After I approve, fix only the causes confirmed in Steps 1–3 and add a test covering each one.

Step 5 (independent check): Verify the fixed calculation directly against raw source records or an independent check outside your new unit tests, show the output, and note anything still uncovered.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Checks a PostgreSQL database from raw sources up — recomputing key figures, running cross-table sanity checks, spotting duplicate entities, and fixing only proven shared causes.
recipes.when: Important numbers in a Postgres database must be verified before anyone relies on them.
steps: rebuild key figures from raw inputs and test cross-table totals (read-only)
check for split/merged records and retroactive rule changes (read-only)
apply targeted fixes plus repeatable SQL/metric checks after approval
show before/after recomputed examples and state any remaining source limits
recipes.copy:
Is the data actually right? Verify key PostgreSQL figures against original sources before changing anything.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay read-only during Steps 1, 2, and 4 — never edit production data, schemas, or app code until I approve Step 3.

Step 1 (prove numbers and cross-check tables — read-only): Pick representative important figures and independently reconstruct them from raw sources without trusting existing calculation code. Also test cross-table totals, accounting identities, plausible ranges, and source coverage for data that passes constraints yet is analytically wrong. Bring back: independent rebuilds, failed cross-table reconciliations, affected row counts, and shared causes (file:line). Stop if the database stores only raw entries with no derived figures.

Step 2 (identity & history — read-only, run only if Step 1 points here): Check whether real-world entities (customers, companies, products) were duplicated or wrongly merged across imports, and whether today's rules rewrite past records' historical meaning. Bring back: concrete duplicate/merge examples with the matching rule (file:line), or past records whose meaning shifted.

Step 3 (targeted fix): After I approve, fix only the confirmed shared causes and add SQL or metric regression tests for them.

Step 4 (proof): Show recomputed examples that now match their sources, how many records were affected, and any source gaps stated plainly.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Maps everything writing to your Postgres tables, traces one full import end to end, trims redundant steps and no-op writes, and keeps retries safe.
recipes.when: Postgres imports are slow, expensive, fragile on retry, or unnecessarily multi-staged.
steps: Map writers & trace one full import
see every writer and cut redundant stages (read-only)
Check no-op writes, safe reruns & rule ownership
measure unchanged rewrites, test retries, and untangle split validation (read-only / separate copy)
Apply one simplification at a time
keep provenance and correction support intact
prove identical output, less write work, and safe retries on a separate test database
recipes.copy:
Make ingestion simpler and cheaper. Cut wasted Postgres import work without losing source traceability or safe retries.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay read-only during Steps 1 and 2. Anything that changes state (replays or rebuild tests) runs only on a separate database with safe test data, never on production.

Step 1 (map writers & trace one import — read-only): Map every script, job, API, trigger, and function that writes to the target tables, flagging conflicting writers. Then trace one complete import from raw source to final rows to spot redundant parsing, staging tables, duplicate validation, and extra writes. Bring back: a writer map (file:line), one full import trace, and the simplest path that keeps provenance and recovery checkpoints.

Step 2 (churn, retries & split rules — read-only / test copy, run only what applies): Check what share of writes rewrite unchanged rows, whether retries or out-of-order files duplicate/corrupt data (never trusting ON CONFLICT alone), and whether validation rules are duplicated across app code and SQL triggers. Bring back: unchanged-write share, unsafe retry cases (file:line), and clearest rule ownership.

Step 3 (incremental fix): After I approve, simplify one confirmed bottleneck at a time while preserving provenance, intentional timestamps, and correction handling.

Step 4 (verify on a test copy): Prove on a separate database that reference inputs produce identical records with measurably fewer writes and safe reruns.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Inventories unused Postgres views, triggers, functions, and duplicate tables, untangles confusing names, and verifies safe rollout before retiring anything.
recipes.when: Your Postgres schema has accumulated old views, triggers, and redundant tables nobody dares to delete.
steps: map tables, views, triggers, functions, and real callers (read-only)
find drifting copies and misleading names (read-only)
verify old and new app versions coexist and test migrations on a separate database
remove complexity with unchanged results for users
recipes.copy:
Simplify a crowded schema. Retire unused PostgreSQL objects and duplicate storage without breaking live readers.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay read-only during Steps 1–3. Any migration replay runs only on a separate database with safe test data, never on production.

Step 1 (inventory objects & consumers — read-only): List tables, views, materialized views, triggers, functions, and indexes that look obsolete or redundant, verifying real consumers including dynamic queries and external readers. Bring back: dependency map, ranked removal candidates, and migration risk. Stop if the schema is small and every object has a known reader.

Step 2 (duplicate facts & naming — read-only, if needed): Check for facts maintained in multiple tables/views that can drift apart, and misleading table or column names causing real bugs or agent errors (skip cosmetic renames). Bring back: authoritative vs. duplicate stores and low-risk boundary fixes.

Step 3 (pre-merge safety check — read-only / test copy): Before removing or changing any object, verify existing records stay intact, running app versions survive rollout, locks are safe, and a real rollback exists. Replay the migration on a separate test database.

Step 4 (apply approved removals): After I approve, ship the smallest safe cleanup and confirm unchanged outputs for users and queries.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Measures which Postgres tables, indexes, queries, and write loops actually drive your bill, cuts the biggest measured waste first, and verifies savings.
recipes.when: Your Postgres compute, storage, or hosting bill is climbing faster than your product's growth.
steps: measure top storage, CPU, bloat, and unused indexes (read-only)
Drill into write churn or scaling queries
inspect unchanged rewrites and slow query plans (read-only)
Take the top measured saving first
skip speculative indexes or premature partitioning
compare workload metrics with zero loss of correctness
recipes.copy:
Reduce PostgreSQL resource cost. Cut measured database waste without breaking queries or adding speculative complexity.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay read-only during Steps 1, 2, and 4 — never edit production data, indexes, or queries until I approve Step 3.

Step 1 (measure waste — read-only): Measure which tables, indexes, queries, and maintenance tasks consume the most storage, CPU, and write I/O (unused indexes, bloat, dead tuples, full scans). Bring back: table/index sizes, top statements, index usage counts, EXPLAIN plans, and estimated savings. Stop if usage and cost are already small and flat.

Step 2 (churn & scaling — read-only, run only what Step 1 points to): Measure unchanged row rewrites in write-heavy jobs, and inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans for queries growing badly with row count. Bring back: write-churn share and query plans with realistic row counts.

Step 3 (apply top measured fix): After I approve, implement only the highest-saving measured fix. No speculative indexes or premature partitioning.

Step 4 (verify): Report before-and-after query plans, write/storage figures, and confirmation that query results remain identical.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Verifies a risky database migration before deploy — or tests rebuilding/restoring your Postgres database on a separate copy — before anything touches production.
recipes.when: You are about to ship a breaking schema change, or you have never tested recovering your database.
steps: Audit the pending migration or rebuild path
inspect rollout safety or source-rebuild completeness (read-only)
verify draining workers, locks, and interrupted transactions (read-only)
run the migration or restore drill on an isolated copy with safe test data
verify tested results with zero unproved claims about production
recipes.copy:
Ship or recover safely. Verify a PostgreSQL migration or database rebuild on a separate copy before trusting it in production.

Run these steps one at a time. Wait for my yes after each step. Stay read-only on production at all times — every migration replay or restore test runs only on a separate database with safe test data, never on production.

Step 1 (audit change or rebuild — read-only): For a pending migration, review the diff against the live schema, active consumers, locks, old/new version coexistence, and rollback realism (reverting app code alone is not a schema rollback). For disaster recovery, audit whether the database can be rebuilt from repo migrations, source files, and backups, flagging anything that exists only in production. Bring back: concrete gaps and risks (file:line).

Step 2 (deploy window & partial failures — read-only, if needed): Trace what happens while old client bundles or background workers are still draining during deploy, and check transaction/timeout paths that could leave half-committed data. Bring back: any compatibility break or half-committed failure path (file:line).

Step 3 (isolated rehearsal): On a separate test database only, execute the migration (and rollback plan) or full rebuild/restore, and compare sampled rows and queries before and after.

Step 4 (go/no-go summary): Report what the isolated test proved, any remaining risks or manual steps, and whether it is safe to proceed.

Start your report in plain English: what you found, what it means, and whether I need to do anything. Put files, lines and commands underneath.

recipes.line: Checks the five things solo builders forget before opening a product to the public: accounts, outgoing emails, public links and previews, likely support questions, and outage alerts.
recipes.when: The product works for you locally and you are about to share it publicly for the first time.
steps: make sure strangers can get in, reset passwords, and not get stuck
check links, wording, sender config, and double sends
check titles, share cards, favicons, error pages, and crawl rules
catch confusing screens and dead ends before people email you
make sure an outage reaches you before a customer tells you

home.title: Things to give your coding agent
home.lede: For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent working on your project. Start from what's wrong, or browse the three kinds.

Prompts.def: Text you copy and paste. Works in any agent.
Prompts.more: Rules that make the agent more careful on any request, and investigations that check one thing about your project and report back without changing it.
Prompts.eg: For example: Prove it wrong · Show the plan and wait · Follow one dollar

Skills.def: Commands you type, such as /keen. Most need Agent Kit installed.
Skills.more: Each runs a whole job the same way every time. Any /keen job can also be copied as plain instructions for an agent without Agent Kit.

Recipes.def: Prompts and skills in order, for a bigger job.
Recipes.more: Run one step at a time and read the result before the next.
Recipes.eg: For example: Fix a screen that feels off · A bug you can't explain

ledes.prompts: Text you paste into any agent. Nothing to install. Investigations check your project and report back without changing files.
ledes.skills: Commands you type in your agent. Each needs its Agent Kit plugin. Without Agent Kit, open any /keen job and copy its full instructions instead.
ledes.recipes: A bigger job as prompts and skills in order. Some copy as one prompt for a single chat. The ones with commands or several investigations run one step per message, each with its own Copy.
